title: Talent Mobility 101: Strategies for a Thriving and Adaptable Workforce
teaser: Unlock business growth with effective talent mobility. Discover strategies, overcome barriers, and implement best practices for a thriving workforce.
bodyText:
Talent mobility  is increasingly becoming a fundamental aspect of  strategic human resource management , designed to nurture and retain top talent within an organization. It's a dynamic approach that goes beyond traditional career progression models, encouraging and facilitating the movement of employees across different roles, functions, or departments. By leveraging the  internal talent marketplace , companies can effectively align individual aspirations with organizational needs, unlocking a symbiotic growth path for both. This  organizational agility  isn't just about filling vacancies; it's about understanding and leveraging the skills, experiences, and career interests of the workforce to foster innovation and adaptability. Instituting a robust talent mobility program can lead to substantial benefits, from increased job satisfaction and employee engagement to improved succession planning and talent retention. By investing in the development of their workforce, organizations can build a more responsive, skilled, and committed team ready to rise to the challenges of a rapidly evolving business environment. Key takeaways Talent mobility enhances the alignment of employee skills with organizational needs. A focus on internal career mobility opportunities can result in higher engagement and retention. Strategic mobility practices foster innovation and adaptability in the workforce. Understanding talent mobility In today's dynamic work environment, the concept of talent mobility has become pivotal in harnessing the full potential of a workforce and fostering a culture of continual growth and learning. What is internal talent mobility? Internal talent mobility refers to the movement of employees within an organization across different roles, departments, or geographic locations. It's a strategic approach  that promotes the optimal use of an employee's skills and talents where they can serve best.  Benefits of embracing internal mobility When you embrace talent mobility, you reap significant rewards. Productivity takes a leap forward  as employees engage in roles that maximize their skill sets. Here’s a snapshot of the benefits: Growth Opportunities:  Employees have the chance to expand their expertise and take on new challenges, leading to a more fulfilling career path. Employee Engagement:  A dynamic internal career landscape keeps the job exciting, boosting morale and deepening commitment to your company. Increased productivity:  Employees in roles that match their strengths tend to be more efficient and innovative, driving better business outcomes. Retention:  An upward trajectory within the organization can decrease turnover rates as employees see a future with your company, making it easier to  attract and retain talent .   By implementing a talent mobility program, you encourage a resilient workforce that is proficient, motivated, and aligned with your organization's goals. Strategic initiatives for successful talent mobility  Implementing strategic initiatives is essential to enhance your organization's talent mobility. A talent mobility strategy ensures employees are continuously developing and can move within the company to meet both their career goals and your business needs. Developing a talent mobility strategy Strategy is at the core of promoting talent mobility. Start by aligning your talent mobility strategy with business objectives to ensure that it contributes to your company’s growth. Objectives might include improving  employee retention strategies , filling skill gaps, or fostering innovative thinking. Define clear policies  and develop a framework for talent mobility that encompasses employee aspirations, skill development, and the company’s strategic goals. Career pathing and development programs Talent  management relies heavily on identifying and nurturing your workforce's career paths. Establish  learning and development programs  that offer a variety of opportunities tailored to the individual goals and competencies of your employees. Encouraging career pathing ensures that your team members understand their potential career trajectories within the organization and are equipped with the skills to navigate their journeys successfully. Implementing talent mobility task forces Forming a talent mobility task force is a proactive approach to driving these strategies effectively. This dedicated team will be responsible for managing your internal talent pipelines, facilitating internal mobility opportunities, and measuring the success of initiatives. 
An effective task force often involves cross-functional stakeholders who can champion career mobility across various departments and ensure alignment with the overall  talent management strategy framework.   Overcoming barriers to mobility Enhancing talent mobility within your organization involves navigating through several critical barriers—ranging from skill deficits to rigid corporate cultures. With the right strategies and tools, you can transform these obstacles into opportunities for growth and improved performance. Identifying and addressing skills gaps  In our  Global Human Resource Index  survey, 63% of those surveyed in the UK indicated they collaborated with individuals whose  skills did not match their present position . In the US, this percentage increased to 64%, and in Ireland, it climbed to 70%.    To effectively address  skills gaps  and build future workforce capability, it's vital to understand the specific competencies needed within your organization.  Assessing employee skills  and comparing them against future business needs can uncover areas requiring development.  Proactive measures like targeted training can help bridge these gaps, ensuring your employees are prepared to step into new roles as needed. For more insights, explore how to overcome barriers to talent mobility. Creating inclusive and diverse workplaces A diverse workforce brings a multitude of perspectives and ideas, fostering innovation and resilience. Making  inclusivity  a cornerstone of your company’s culture starts by recruiting from a variety of backgrounds and promoting an environment where all employees feel valued and heard. Constructive dialogues and inclusive policies pave the way for every individual to achieve their potential. To delve further, consider the significance of building a talent mobility culture.  Leveraging technology and infrastructure Technology  plays a crucial role in modernizing talent mobility. Utilizing digital tools and software can simplify internal processes, improve communication, and provide data-driven insights to aid decision-making. Moreover, the right  infrastructure —both physical and digital—supports a dynamic work environment where talent can move fluidly to where it's most needed. Discover methods to integrate technology into talent mobility strategies by examining effective talent mobility programs. Talent mobility program best practices In any thriving organization, the emphasis on developing and retaining skilled employees is paramount. Implementing best practices in talent mobility is a direct investment in the company's future and the fulfillment of its employees' potential. Promoting from within Promotion from within  not only boosts morale but also leverages the deep understanding and experience that existing employees have with your company's culture and processes. To support this, create clear career pathways and ensure that your promotions are highly visible to encourage others. Fostering a culture of lifelong learning A culture that prizes  lifelong learning  is essential in facilitating talent mobility. By providing access to continuous learning opportunities, such as workshops and online courses, you enable employees to expand their skill sets, making them more adaptable and better equipped for different roles within your organization. Enhancing internal communication and collaboration Effective  internal communication  and  collaboration  are the glue that holds the moving parts of talent mobility together. Foster an environment where cross-department communication is the norm and cooperation is encouraged through regular team meetings and the use of collaborative tools. Measuring and enhancing mobility outcomes In talent mobility, success is gauged by the achievement of desired outcomes and the satisfaction of your employees. By tracking key metrics and leveraging feedback, you can enhance both the effectiveness and the experience of mobility programs. Tracking mobility metrics and employee satisfaction To truly understand the impact of talent mobility initiatives, you need to monitor a set of  clearly defined metrics . This might include: Performance:  Look at the contributions of employees who have moved into new roles or locations. Engagement:  Measure the levels of enthusiasm and commitment in your mobile workforce. Retention:  Keep tabs on how often employees stay with your company after a mobility experience. Promotion Rates:  Track the career progression of employees who have been mobile within the company.  Continuous improvement through feedback loops Feedback is the cornerstone of continuous improvement. Establish  feedback loops  that enable employees to share insights about their mobility experiences. This might involve: Pre- and Post-Move Surveys:  Collect data on the expectations and actual experiences of mobile employees. Regular Check-Ins:  Encourage ongoing dialogue between employees and mobility managers. Exit Interviews:  For those who leave, understanding their reasons can be invaluable. Act on the feedback you receive to refine your processes. This could include: Training Programs:  Enhance support for cultural integration or skills development. Policy Adjustments:  Make changes to better meet the needs and preferences of your workforce. A focus on outcomes, employee satisfaction, metrics, and feedback is not only about enhancing the mobility program. It's about ensuring  you thrive in today's dynamic talent landscape . Use the data and opinions you collect to foster an environment where mobility is not just supported but celebrated as a key to personal and organizational growth. Conclusion In the evolving landscape of strategic human resource management, talent mobility emerges as a pivotal force for unlocking the symbiotic growth of both employees and organizations.  By fostering a culture that champions internal mobility, companies not only align individual aspirations with organizational goals but also cultivate a workforce that is adaptable, skilled, and deeply committed to the company's success.  This dynamic approach to career progression—encouraging movement across roles, functions, or departments—ensures that organizations remain agile and innovative in the face of rapid business changes.  Implementing robust talent mobility programs leads to enhanced job satisfaction, increased employee engagement, and improved talent retention, thereby securing a competitive edge in today's fast-paced business environment.  In essence, talent mobility is not just a strategy for filling vacancies; it's a comprehensive approach to nurturing a resilient, motivated, and future-ready workforce.

title: What is Talent Management? Definition, Strategy, and Process
teaser: Discover the importance of effective talent management in order to optimize the talent lifecycle, empower your workforce, and enhance business performance.
bodyText: Employee recruitment and retention are central to a business's success. What does it take to find and hold on to talented employees?  A    found that 35% of workers who recently left their jobs said that they quit because their employers didn't care about them. In addition, the majority of respondents listed a  lack of career development and advancement as the top reason for leaving their jobs. Effective  talent management  addresses both of these concerns, building a positive environment with engaged leadership and meaningful work. To develop strong talent management, you first need to understand what it involves, why it matters, and how to create a program that motivates workers to join your company, fulfill their potential, and stay with you for the long term. What is talent management? Talent management refers to the processes that HR uses to recruit, develop, support, and retain an effective and engaged workforce. The goal is to improve organizational performance by bringing on and retaining top-quality talent. Although it can encompass a wide range of practices, talent management primarily focuses on these tasks:  Talent management affects HR from every angle, requiring you to leverage a variety of resources and enhance your strategies to achieve your organization's objectives. It also addresses some of your biggest  challenges in HR,  including problems with retention and performance management.  Importance of talent management in HR The importance of talent management ties directly to your organization's overall performance. These are some of the most favorable outcomes businesses see when they invest in their employees' well-being, development, and success. Attracting and retaining top talent Poor hiring decisions are expensive , with one study estimating that a single    on average. That number increases based on the individual's salary and the prominence of their role. Finding the right person for a position the first time thus saves your company not only money but also time and resources, which are equally valuable. High-performing job candidates are drawn to companies that prioritize talent management, making it key to attracting and retaining effective employees. As part of your talent management program, you'll refine your approach to recruitment and  find ways to identify talent gaps  in your existing workforce.   A strategic and intentional process with these components will position your company as an appealing employment option, allowing you to find high-quality talent that understands and fulfills your needs. Driving organizational performance Another facet of talent management is creating robust training and development for your employees. These programs empower your team to build on their skills, motivate them to continue improving and keep them engaged. A    found that 70% of workers agree that training and upskilling improved their satisfaction at work. Better employee training contributes to stronger retention, which means fewer financial losses and disruptions. Well-managed talent will also produce more consistent and higher-quality work, leading to greater profitability.   On top of those advantages, a  talent management program gives you the opportunity to identify future leaders  for your company. Through your performance management system, you'll observe employees' strengths and help expand on them. Up-and-coming leaders are essential to your company's market competitiveness and long-term success. Promoting a strong organizational culture Effective talent management fosters a positive and supportive organizational culture that emphasizes collaboration, innovation, and inclusivity.  For example, mentoring programs help employees build trust from their earliest days with the company. Using talent management tools and activities such as discussion forums, virtual meetings, and shared resources encourages employees to work together and rely on one another. Your talent management program can also promote inclusivity, especially if you commit to  hiring a more diverse workforce.  Companies can offer training on issues such as unconscious bias, which can create tension and anxiety in the workplace, particularly for employees from marginalized groups.  Enhancing agility and innovation Creating a more agile organization that can adapt quickly to changes in the market is critical for any business that wants to survive unexpected disruptions and upheaval. You never know when you'll face the next surprise, whether it's a global health crisis, war, or natural disaster.  Through your talent management program and  skills matrix , you can address skill gaps in advance, ensuring employees are ready to pivot as the market, technology, and customer expectations evolve.  You can also   use a  talent intelligence platform  to collect data and target necessary changes in your workforce, such as determining which roles might need to encompass new responsibilities to adapt to shifts in the market. Improving the overall employee experience Talent management can create a more positive employee experience at every stage, from onboarding through professional development.  Organizations with a better employee experience see greater productivity, sales, and engagement. As a result, helping employees nurture the skills that will drive their success is beneficial for everyone. For example,  offering feedback and coaching helps workers find their strengths and identify a fulfilling career path . Rewarding their accomplishments and prioritizing their well-being helps them stay healthy, happy, and motivated. Employees with these characteristics will feel inspired to work harder and will develop a greater sense of loyalty to your company. How to create a successful HR talent management system Some businesses don't invest in their talent strategies because they aren't sure where to begin. These steps will help you establish a strong foundation that you can continue to build upon. 1. Identify strategic business priorities The first step in developing your talent management process is understanding your company's strategic priorities. Think of short and long-term goals because they will both influence the success of your program and your organization's performance. Aligning your talent management efforts with your business priorities ensures that HR initiatives drive the outcomes you want to achieve. 2. Define key components of your strategy Breaking down the core components of your  talent management and development strategy  makes it easier to understand what you want to accomplish and how you can make it happen. For example, rather than taking a broad perspective of your program, break down your organization's plans for recruitment, employee development, performance management, and succession planning.  3. Establish roles and responsibilities The team responsible for your  talent management might include HR professionals  as well as managers, recruiters, and other employees. Clearly defining their roles and responsibilities is crucial. Determine who will serve as leaders and how other team members will support them in designing and implementing your strategy.  This ensures that the right people have the responsibilities that are the best match for them and know exactly what they should be doing at any given time. While these individual roles are vital, the talent management team can only function if there's cross-functional collaboration and leadership involvement. This ensures that the team stays aligned and accountable and that the process remains on track throughout every stage of your program. 4. Implement supporting systems and technology The growing role of  technology in human resource management  also extends to your talent management program. As you develop your strategy, identify and implement the HR technologies and systems that will streamline your processes. They might include talent management software and analytics tools, which offer you a deeper look into your employees, their performance, and what's lacking in your current team. Features like automation, data tracking, and real-time insights help optimize various aspects of your talent management program, including recruitment, performance evaluations, and employee development. For example, software that allows you to  track your team's progress  through a training program makes it easy for you to identify areas that might require additional explanation or employees who need extra support. 5. Set measurable goals and KPIs To ensure that your talent management process is working as it should, you'll need to establish clear, measurable goals and key performance indicators (KPIs) from the outset. Some of the metrics you might track include:  Employee retention Engagement  Performance  Employee satisfaction Talent mobility  These data points allow you to evaluate your strategy and pinpoint areas for improvement objectively.  6. Align with company culture and values Some companies falter because their talent management practices don't align with the larger organization's values. When an employee completes onboarding or training, they experience culture shock, discovering that the atmosphere of the workplace is drastically different from their initial perception.  This  disjointed transition can result in higher turnover rates , lower motivation, and lacking engagement. A cohesive employee experience, on the other hand, helps you move employees smoothly from recruitment to retention. 7. Regularly review and adjust Even companies with highly successful talent management programs must continuously conduct  talent management reviews  and adjust their strategies. This is the only way to ensure that your approach remains relevant and effective as the market and the candidate population change.  As part of this process, you can collect feedback from employees and applicants, analyze performance data, and adapt to changes in business goals or workforce needs. For example,  Gallup's survey on hybrid work  shows that in an era when more than half of eligible workers want a hybrid work environment, many companies have made adjustments to their expectations for remote and on-site attendance.  The four best talent management strategies Developing or refining a talent management system is an intensive process that becomes less overwhelming when you start with a framework. Many businesses rely on these four talent management models to guide their practices.  The AARRR model (Acquisition, Activation, Revenue, Referral, Retention) Also known as the Pirate Metrics model, the AARRR model's original purpose was to conceptualize the customer journey, but some businesses also apply it to the employee journey. In this model, employees undergo five stages of employment:  This model provides a structured approach to maximizing employee value at every step of the employee life cycle,  helping you build a stronger and more lasting workforce .  The traditional 5-stage talent management model The five-stage model is similar to the AARRR model, but it features slightly different stages:   Strategic workforce planning : establishing your goals Attraction: developing and using strategies to attract talent Onboarding: creating effective onboarding and preparing employees to grow within the company  Retention: maintaining employee engagement  Transitioning: supporting employees who want to advance within and outside of the company and holding effective exit interviews  As the stages reflect, this model emphasizes smooth transitions and knowledge transfers between employees, helping your organization to navigate changes within the workforce.  The integrated talent management model As the name suggests, the integrated talent management model focuses on bringing together an array of HR processes, including:  Recruitment  Onboarding Performance management  Learning and development  Succession planning  This model recognizes that HR teams, organizational leaders, and recruiters have historically worked independently of one another. The model encourages an interconnected approach that  improves retention , provides more actionable data, and paints a clearer picture of the entire employee experience.  The modern talent management model The modern talent management model emphasizes building a diverse workforce and fostering an inclusive environment. It recognizes that a workplace that values and respects all employees, regardless of their backgrounds, is more productive and promotes higher morale.  As such, businesses using this model should take an intentional approach to recruitment, seeking ways to attract diverse candidates and taking advantage of  HR industry trends  like technology and data analytics to support decision-making. Talent management best practices Every organization is unique, so there's no one-size-fits-all solution to talent management. However, these proven best practices will help you create a successful talent management program that supports prospective and existing employees, as well as your organization as a whole, by  enhancing employee engagement  and achieving alignment with company goals. Prioritize diversity and inclusion in the workforce Making diversity and inclusion a core tenet of your organization and your talent management strategy can improve organizational performance and enhance the employee experience. Aim to make intelligent, informed decisions when hiring and recruiting and recognize that diverse teams are critical to innovation.   Research has found  that having a diverse workforce in healthcare settings improved patient outcomes, financial performance, and adaptability to change.  Foster an employer brand to attract top talent Prospective employees are drawn to companies that are known for having a solid culture and values, and you can convey that message by building your employer brand. This makes it easier to fill positions with high-caliber candidates and retain them over time.  Your performance management and employee recognition programs are central to this effort. Consider including them in your job descriptions, online company profiles, and social media posts, and highlight them when interviewing job candidates. Another effective strategy is to develop an employee referral program that rewards workers for successful referrals. Finally, remember that happy and engaged employees are more likely to speak positively about your company in public, which is another vital way to strengthen your employer's brand.    Ensure continuous performance management A    found that almost half of companies in the United States give employees annual or semiannual reviews, and 7% offer no feedback at all. While an annual review is better than nothing, it also allows errors to become habits and slows the employee's growth.  Align talent strategy with business objectives Your talent management strategy should directly align with the broader goals of your organization. In addition to creating a more consistent representation of your business, this alignment also helps drive overall company performance. As a result, your talent management team and organizational leaders can work together to accomplish key priorities and achieve long-term success. Use data and analytics to inform decisions While you might base some talent management decisions on general principles and a broad understanding of your company's requirements, it's also essential to leverage  innovations in HR , including data and talent analytics. Foster a culture of feedback and recognition To remain engaged and invested in their work, employees need a feedback-rich environment with regular constructive input from leadership.  According to a  report from Gallup , employees who receive authentic recognition are five times more likely to feel connected to the company's culture and four times more likely to feel engaged.  Workhuman's Conversations®  platform makes it easy to collect and request continuous feedback, giving employees a place to reflect on their growth and plan for their development.    Examples of talent management processes in action The concept of talent management may seem relatively straightforward, but it's not always easy to visualize it in practice. These talent management examples of real-world companies with successful strategies can help resolve those uncertainties. Talent management at World Vision World Vision Canada puts employee satisfaction front and center in their talent management. They use an "employee delight index" to see how employees are responding to their workplace environment. They also launched a training program with agile tools to promote self-empowerment and encourage ongoing development. Salesforce's focus on diversity Salesforce has made an ongoing commitment to diversity and inclusion by increasing its representation of under-represented populations. As a result, they've seen an increase in employee engagement and satisfaction, as well as improved business outcomes. Salesforce recently reached a goal of having  50% of its U.S. workforce  identifying as an underrepresented group.  Hyatt Hotels’ approach to talent management  Hospitality company Hyatt Hotels has increasingly focused on employee engagement by striving to empower, recognize, and include team members of all kinds, as highlighted in the article    by the Talent Management Institute.   They've developed a learner app so employees can access resources and courses at any time, expanded their on-the-job training, and introduced mandatory inclusive leadership programs for managers.  Walmart’s talent management strategy Walmart takes a skills-based approach to talent management, recognizing that an employee's value lies in their experience, not just in holding a degree. Their talent strategy focuses on developing current employees into new roles within the company, and they introduced a "career explorer" to educate workers about potential roles based on their interests, skills, and goals. Pulling it all together Effective talent management is at the heart of thriving companies with strong productivity and performance. To enhance your operations and develop an engaged and motivated workforce, create a program that centers around continuous feedback, diversity and inclusion, data-based decision-making, and alignment with your overall business goals.  This approach has the potential to transform your HR strategy, allowing you to recruit the best possible talent, offer them opportunities for growth, and keep them on board long into the future.

title: The Talent Management Lifecycle: Stages, Strategies, and Best Practices
teaser: Discover how the talent management lifecycle helps HR teams improve hiring, development, retention and long-term workforce planning.
bodyText: A competitor has spirited away another high performer, and your oh-so-promising new hire takes six months to contribute. Oh, and you've interviewed 12 people for that critical role, but no one has the exact skills you need. Sound familiar? By focusing on the  talent management lifecycle , you can connect these seemingly disconnected problems into a system you can actually fix. It's how you move talent decisions from reactive firefighting to deliberate planning across every stage of employment, from workforce planning through offboarding. Skills’ half-lives are shrinking, and ManpowerGroup’s insights on “  ” say that up to 74% of employers struggle to fill roles. Meanwhile, an Express Employment Professionals-Harris Poll survey, “The $100,000/Year Drain: How Employee Turnover Is Costing Companies Big in 2025”, found that turnover costs businesses an average of $36,723 annually.  But it's not all hopeless. With the  right talent management , you can solve your hiring woes and stay competitive. This guide walks you through all  seven stages of the lifecycle  and explains the difference between talent management and basic HR administration (hint: it's more strategic and future-facing). It also gives you a practical roadmap to start using this framework in your organization. What is the talent management lifecycle?  The talent lifecycle can also make a huge difference in the employee experience. According to Deloitte’s “The skills-based organization: A new operating model for work and the workforce”, organizations that focus on helping employees build skills are 98% more likely to retain top performers and 107% more likely to use their talent effectively.  While no single platform owns every stage of the talent management lifecycle, recognition and feedback data can strengthen decisions across the entire journey. Workhuman adds a  human-centered layer  of insight by capturing moments of contribution, collaboration, feedback, and appreciation as they happen.  These signals help HR leaders better understand engagement, skills, visibility, performance patterns, and emerging leadership potential alongside the structured data in their HRIS, ATS, LMS, and performance systems.  Key goals of the talent management lifecycle The talent management model is a deliberate strategy that aims to make sure your  organization always has the right skills , when and where you need them. Let's say your leadership team plans to launch an AI initiative in six months. With the lifecycle, you can start recruiting AI specialists now or upskilling your current employees instead of racing to hire people at the time when the business outcomes should have come. Other goals include: Creating a more positive employee experience Decreasing time-to-productivity for new hires Developing succession plans for critical roles, such as executives and managers Improving overall productivity Making HR decisions that match the business goals and strategy Raising performance through clear feedback and growth opportunities Reducing turnover costs by proactively fixing retention issues Supporting long-term employee growth and promoting from within Talent management vs. human resource management  Talent management falls under the umbrella of  human resource management (HRM) , but there are a few key differences:  Of course, you don't have to choose one or the other. Effective organizations usually have strong HR operations and a clear talent lifecycle. Plus,  talent management relies on HRM data and processes  for many decisions. For instance, you may analyze performance data to see which teams need more support or where a new hire would make the biggest impact. Talent management lifecycle vs. employee lifecycle HR professionals often talk about employee and talent management lifecycles when discussing workforce planning. Here's a quick comparison:  For the best results, use the employee lifecycle to map out core processes and stages. Layer your talent management strategy on top to make sure you're supporting and engaging your team at every step.  Why the talent management lifecycle matters now more than ever If you feel like you get whiplash every time you read HR news, you're not alone. The workforce looks very different from it did a decade ago, and organizations can no longer count on a simple "help wanted" sign whenever they need to hire. Here are six trends reshaping HR and how a talent management strategy can help: AI and automation : While anyone can experiment with ChatGPT, more advanced AI knowledge remains scarce. In the World Economic Forum survey, “AI’s new dual workforce challenge: Balancing overcapacity and talent shortages”, the majority (94%) of leaders say they're experiencing an AI-critical skills shortage. The talent lifecycle can address this gap by allowing organizations to upskill or reskill tech-savvy employees. It can also help companies make smart decisions about which tasks to automate and how to redesign roles to make the most of top talent.   Talent scarcity : The saying "good help is hard to find" has never been more true. A 2025 US Talent Shortage Survey by ManpowerGroup found that many employers are struggling to fill roles in information technology, operations, sales, and other key areas. Focusing on retention and reskilling can help address this skills shortage. Growth of remote and hybrid work : At most organizations, the office looks emptier than usual these days. According to Robert Half’s “Remote work statistics and trends for 2026” report, 88% of employers offer at least some hybrid options, and 12% of new job postings in the third quarter of 2025 were fully remote. This shift has helped expand talent pools, but it's also led to fierce competition for top performers. If you want employees to flock to your company and stick around, you need to prioritize culture-building and employee engagement. Rising turnover costs : Replacing an employee can cost the equivalent of a significant percentage of their annual salary. By reducing attrition, talent management decreases hiring expenses. Strategic advantages : According to McKinsey’s “What is talent management?”, organizations with very effective talent management are more likely to outperform competitors. It can also help businesses adapt to change by making sure employees have the right skills for what comes next.  The evolution of talent management: From personnel administration to strategic advantage  While businesses have always relied on employees, the way they manage their workforce has changed drastically over the past 60 years. Here's a brief timeline of this evolution, according to an Open Access Library Journal article titled, “  ”: 1950s-1970s : Personnel management primarily focused on administrative tasks, such as payroll and record-keeping. Employers often viewed their teams as expenses, not resources. 1980s-1990s : Businesses adopted a strategic human resources management approach. They viewed people practices as part of their overall strategy and prioritized employee development. 2000s : Organizations began viewing HR as a strategic partner and focused on attracting and keeping high performers. McKinsey coined the term "The War for Talent" to describe this shift. 2010s : The growing popularity of  people analytics in HR  allowed organizations to make data-driven talent decisions. Today, skills-based hiring is the latest trend reshaping HR. According to a Workday survey, “The Global State of Skills,” 55% of businesses have already transitioned to this model. Other emerging trends include AI-assisted recruiting and internal talent marketplaces, which help match current employees to new roles. See also:  13 Best People Analytics Software in [current_year]   The 7 key stages of the talent management lifecycle There are several models for talent lifecycle management, but it typically covers a few core activities. Stage 1: Workforce planning Before you start brainstorming job ads, you need to understand your current workforce. Inventory your team's skills and roles, and  look for potential gap s that could affect your future business plans. For example, a tech company might realize that no one has experience with a new programming language needed for an upcoming project.  Stage 2: Recruitment and attraction Stellar performers usually don't fall into your lap. Follow these steps to  attract and retain top talent :  Spell out what your ideal candidate looks like based on your current and future needs. If your organization's three-year plan involves using more data analytics, look for people who already have those skills, even if you don't need them right now. Don't just rely on LinkedIn for recruitment. Source candidates through several channels, including referrals and industry job boards. Once you've identified a few promising candidates, evaluate fit with a structured interview and skills assessments. Make competitive offers with fair compensation and benefits. Emphasize growth opportunities and other perks, such as flexible start times and hybrid schedules. Gather data to measure the effectiveness of your talent acquisition lifecycle.  Stage 3: Onboarding It's tempting to rush through onboarding. After all, you're excited about your new hires and want them to start contributing as soon as possible. However, the Work Institute’s 2025 retention report states that early attrition makes up 40% of overall turnover. A  strong onboarding program  helps new hires learn the culture, reducing the risk of losing them in the first year. Before employees officially start, send them welcome materials and explain the expectations for their roles. These small gestures can help soothe pre-boarding jitters. During the first week, introduce new employees to key stakeholders and existing employees, and give them opportunities for early wins. This could be as simple as participating in a team meeting or completing a small project. These activities build confidence without overwhelming recruits. Continue checking in with new hires throughout their first 90 days. Set training milestones, and match them with a mentor. Your  new hire onboarding checklist  should also include frequent feedback conversations to get them up to speed quickly. Stage 4: Performance management The work isn't over once new hires start contributing. Throughout their tenure, HR should manage their performance to help them meet expectations and grow. Collaborate with employees to develop  SMART goals  that connect their priorities to the team and the company's objectives. A marketer, for instance, may aim to design a TikTok campaign that boosts engagement by 20% this quarter. Give regular feedback as they work toward these goals. Platforms like Conversations allow you to schedule frequent check-ins with employees instead of waiting for annual reviews. This software can also calibrate formal performance reviews to make sure they're fair and consistent.   These discussions should feel supportive, not scary or punitive. Give employees space to express their goals and concerns, and be clear about expectations. Over time, link performance outcomes to development opportunities and compensation. And make sure to recognize exceptional efforts, too. Stage 5: Learning and development  According to the Gallup study, “Addressing the Barriers Blocking Employee Development”, only 45% of employees participated in training for their current job in 2024. Professional development is a key phase of the talent management cycle because it  keeps employees engaged and prepared to adapt to new role s. These best practices can help you strengthen your team's skill set:  Use human-centered analytics, such as  Workhuman ®  iQ and related talent insights, to identify skills signals, collaboration patterns, and employees who may benefit from targeted development opportunities  Offer leadership development programs and technical upskilling. For example, you might host a monthly workshop on data literacy or automation. Create individual development plans (IDPs) that connect employees' current roles to future career paths. Develop mentorship programs or provide opportunities for one-on-one coaching. Encourage managers to offer stretch assignments to help employees build experience and adjacent skills. Link learning opportunities to succession plans. A leadership boot camp might open the door to a management position. Stage 6: Retention and engagement  Employee Recognition  is one of the most effective ways to encourage employees to stick around. Encourage managers to praise engaged employees, and create a system for peer recognition. Make these acknowledgments even more meaningful with small rewards, such as bonuses or an extra day off. Keep a close eye on engagement, too. Send out regular pulse surveys, and offer opportunities for employees to provide feedback. This data can reveal declining morale or negative sentiment before it leads to attrition. If parents seem disengaged, for instance, you might offer flexible work options or support groups to meet their needs. Finally, use career and retention conversations to  spot potential flight risks . Sometimes, a new role or recognition is all it takes to re-engage dissatisfied employees who are eyeing job ads. Stage 7: Offboarding and redeployment  Even the most supportive organizations offboard employees. These best practices can help you end your relationship on a positive note: Conduct exit interviews and surveys to spot recurring issues and get feedback on improving the talent management lifecycle. If several existing employees say they didn't get enough mentorship, it's time to set up a learning and development program. Create a system for handing off documentation, knowledge, and projects. That way, departures don't disrupt entire teams. If your organization is eliminating certain roles, consider whether you can move the employees instead of offboarding them. Stay in touch with previous employees by building alumni networks or following them on social media. These former employees could refer people to you later or even return as boomerang hires.  Integrating succession planning across stages  Strategic workforce planning  means preparing to fill critical roles long before an employee hands in their resignation letter. If you wait until the offboarding stage, you may scramble to find qualified replacements. Here's how to plan for succession throughout the entire talent management lifecycle: Workforce planning : Create a list of critical roles and future skills you'll need in the next two to three years. Use this information to start building talent pipelines. Recruitment and attraction : As you sort through job applications, look for external hires who have long-term potential. Focus on people with valuable skills you'll need in the future or the ability to develop them. For instance, a data analyst who's already an expert in advanced analytics could probably learn machine learning or new software later. Performance : Flag high performers and track their growth to see when they're ready for next-level roles. Development : Help potential successors grow their skill sets with leadership and specialist programs. That data analyst might be thrilled to go to a leadership workshop or earn a predictive modeling certificate. Retention : Don't leave your best employees in the dark about your plans. Develop concrete growth plans so they can clearly visualize their future with your organization.  This does not replace succession planning. Instead, it complements leadership development by giving organizations a broader, more objective view of future-state leadership talent — including people who may not yet be on the usual shortlist but are already showing signs of influence, impact, and leadership growth. Alternative talent lifecycle models (4-, 5-, and 7-stage)  You don't need to stick to the seven-stage model if it's too complex. Some organizations use a four-stage model, which includes broader phases like  attraction, development, retention, and separation . Or try a five-stage model, which adds another phase for engagement. What matters most is addressing all the key touchpoints, not the exact number of stages.  Talent management lifecycle best practices You don't need to totally overhaul your HR workflows. These practical tips will help you improve your talent lifecycle gradually.  Technology stack for the lifecycle  Even the most competent HR professionals can struggle to remember each employee's goals or sift through a mountain of applications. Luckily, there are plenty of tools to help you stay organized and efficient, such as:  Applicant tracking systems for recruiting  Learning management systems for professional development  Performance management platforms, which make it easy to set goals and exchange feedback Engagement and recognition tools like Workhuman to improve retention People analytics dashboards to monitor metrics throughout the lifecycle  Measuring success: Key metrics by stage  Don't assume your lifecycle is working perfectly. These metrics will help you track your progress at each stage:   Building an employer brand to strengthen talent attraction Stand out from competitors by defining your employee value proposition, or what makes your company a unique place to work. Maybe it's a commitment to sustainability or a fun work culture. Showcase this value through authentic content like employee stories and day-in-the-life videos. The role of HR and people leaders in lifecycle success Collaboration is key to building a strong lifecycle. No single person can manage every stage alone, especially in larger companies. Add these players to your talent management team: HR  designs the lifecycle framework and trains managers. It's also in charge of data analytics. Managers  handle day-to-day activities like giving feedback and helping employees set goals. Senior leadership  focuses on big-picture tasks, such as allocating budget and keeping managers accountable. They set talent priorities, too. Information technology  sets up HR tools and integrates them into your tech stack.  How organizational culture shapes lifecycle effectiveness Your company's culture has a huge impact on the talent lifecycle. If employees feel cynical or view development as a punishment, that negative mindset can make every stage less productive. Avoid this issue by promoting an inclusive, high-trust culture. Celebrate employee achievements, and frame learning as an investment in their future. Leader buy-in is essential, too. How to implement the talent management lifecycle in your organization Follow these steps to put your talent management lifecycle into action:   Common implementation challenges and how to address them It's normal to encounter obstacles as you set up your lifecycle, but proactive planning can help you solve them quickly. Limited resources are one of the most common roadblocks. Get the most out of your budget by prioritizing a few high-impact stages, such as onboarding. Later, you can gradually add more stages. Managers and employees may also resist change, especially if they're anxious that the lifecycle will add to their workloads. Win them over by setting clear expectations and providing training for managers. Rolling out changes slowly can also ease the transition. Real-world examples of successful talent management lifecycles    invested heavily in the talent development cycle. The Starbucks College Achievement plan provides 100% tuition coverage for employees who work at least 20 hours a week. It's also recently announced plans to hire more employees and fill 90% of leadership roles with internal hires. These initiatives have  boosted morale and led to a more energetic company culture. Tools and software to manage the employee lifecycle Technology can help organizations manage the talent lifecycle with more  consistency, visibility, and speed.  In most cases, that means using a connected set of tools rather than a single platform. You might use an applicant tracking system for recruiting, a learning management system for development, performance management software for goal-setting and feedback, and engagement tools to support retention. The real value comes from how well those systems work together. When your tools are disconnected, talent data gets trapped in silos, and employees end up with a fragmented experience. When they’re integrated, HR leaders and managers can make better decisions across the lifecycle, from hiring and onboarding to development, performance, and retention.  Choosing the right platform When evaluating software, start with your biggest pain points. If hiring bottlenecks are slowing growth, recruiting technology may be the priority. If retention or internal mobility is the problem, performance, development, or engagement tools may have a greater impact. These steps can help you choose the right fit: Evaluate your organization’s size, structure, and budget Prioritize the lifecycle stages with the greatest friction or business risk Look for platforms that integrate with your existing HR systems and collaboration tools Request demos based on your real use cases, workflows, and reporting needs Pilot the tool with one team, business unit, or location before expanding further Review implementation support, training resources, and analytics capabilities The best talent technology does more than automate tasks. It helps you connect talent decisions across the employee experience, reduce administrative friction, and give leaders better insight into what employees need to succeed and stay. FAQs  What is the talent management lifecycle? The talent management lifecycle covers all the stages that employees experience as they interact with an organization, from recruitment to retention and offboarding.  How is the talent management process different from human resource management? Talent management is a strategic approach to attracting and supporting employees. On the other hand, human resource management includes all the processes and policies that influence the employee experience, such as payroll and compliance.  What is the goal of the talent management lifecycle? The talent management lifecycle makes sure that organizations have the right talent when they need it.  What is the role of HR in the talent management lifecycle? HR spearheads the talent lifecycle by building the framework, training managers, and supporting employee development.

title: Workhuman vs Reward Gateway -  [current_year]  Comparison Guide
teaser: Reward Gateway vs. Workhuman: Compare features, pricing, integrations, global reach, and impact on employee engagement to choose the right platform.
bodyText: Employee recognition software  is an essential tool for companies to make their employees feel valued and drive engagement. However, different types of software and programs offer distinct benefits based on each company's size, budget, and desired level of insight into its employees' needs.  Both Workhuman and Reward Gateway offer global rewards marketplaces with real-time engagement insights and accessible interfaces to drive long-term performance changes. However, with differing levels of customization, scalability, and reliability, only one may be a good choice for your unique business.   Workhuman vs. Reward Gateway Platform Overview   Workhuman at a Glance  Reward Gateway at a Glance  World-leading award redemption platform , offering employees choice, flexibility, and price transparency (with some limits)  Positions itself as an  all-in-one engagement hub , consolidating several employee-centered needs into one platform, including:  Recognition and rewards  Communication  Surveys  Discounts  Well-being  Emphasizes customization  with branded interfaces, personalized reward options, and Reward Gateway's patented  SmartHub , allowing employers to strategically structure every aspect of recognition experiences  Prioritizes on-the-spot recognition  to support ease-of-use and help frontline employees easily review recognition without disrupting their workflows  Recognition is delivered peer-to-peer and manager-to-employee through eCards and other communication, with tangible rewards connected to nearly every recognition  Different types of rewards, such as cashback, discounts, and vouchers for big-name brands, can make recognition and incentives more appealing  One-step logins and insights with popular workplace tools support ease of use and higher levels of adoption when implemented right  Limited ability to surface meaningful, enterprise-grade insight about:  Recognition reach  Granular reporting  Holistic employee data  The price structure is  suited for enterprise-scale businesses  but too steep for many small and mid-market organizations  Feature Comparison: Workhuman vs. Reward Gateway    Recognition & Culture Building Workhuman   Reward Gateway  The all-in-one engagement structure  combines several essential employee-centered needs to improve recognition insights, build culture, and minimize the administrative platforms you use. These needs include:  Reward and recognition:  The platform's core function is to weave recognition, morale, and support into the company culture.  Employee discounts:  Expand your rewards programs with discounts and vouchers for everyday expenses and popular vendors.  Employee communication:  Support collaboration and communication between distributed and frontline teams.  Employee surveys:  Enable two-way recognition, collect real-time feedback, and use accumulated survey results to track how employee perceptions change over time.  Employee well-being:  Develop well-being programs around employees' diverse needs, with wellness options available around the globe.  Segmented recognition and communication  distinguish employees by their roles, teams, demographics, and needs to help employers deliver personalized messages and support.  Branded platform customizations  let companies redesign the platform's interface around their brand identities and cultures. For example, rather than opening an app that says "Reward Gateway" at the top, employees' dashboards can feature the company's own logos, colors, and videos, enforcing company culture.  User interface (UI) customizations  take personalization further, letting you strategically structure web pages to prioritize what employees see first. Reward Gateway lets you add explainer text, graphics, video content, downloadable documents, and more.  Individual content customization through SmartHub  also lets you dictate which types of recognition content you share with each employee. This allows leaders to respond to each worker's unique achievements, strengths, and gaps.  Social walls  allow users to see their own peer-to-peer shout-outs alongside everyone else's, boosting visibility and feelings of connection.   Integrations & Tech Ecosystem Fit Workhuman  Reward Gateway  As an  all-in-one engagement hub , Reward Gateway reduces the number of employee-centered platforms you need to adopt. It consolidates employee recognition, communication, well-being, surveys, and discounts into a single platform.  Common workplace and collaboration tool integrations  include Slack, Microsoft Teams, Outlook, Azure, Webhooks, Yapster, Workday, SAP SuccessFactors, and Paylocity.  Brand customizations  let you add company colors, logos, and images to Reward Gateway's interface, making it look like a seamless fit within your existing tech ecosystem.  The Reward Gateway SmartInsights Analytics Engine  gives leaders real-time insights into engagement activity and the factors driving performance, with options to customize which metrics you prioritize.  Long-term insights  let leaders track changes in engagement, performance, and other key metrics over time. However, it's unclear how long Reward Gateway stores this information, which can limit insights over time.  Fragmentation  can result in incomplete recognition insights if key employee information is not properly incorporated.     Pricing & Cost-Effectiveness Workhuman  Reward Gateway  A price structure built for enterprise-scale businesses  can impair accessibility and cost-effectiveness for small and mid-market businesses. Many G2 reviews directly reference this issue, noting that there are more affordable options for non-enterprise organizations.  Expiring point systems and reloadable cards  require employees to spend the points they've earned within 60 days or else they'll be forfeited, depending on program settings and reward options. This causes frustration for employees who forget to use their points (or are unaware of the expiration) and ultimately results in wasted funds.   Impact on Engagement, Retention, and Morale Workhuman     Reward Gateway  Frustration with expiring point systems  can negatively impact employee engagement and program adoption. As reflected in customer reviews, some employees would prefer to accumulate points throughout the year for larger rewards, such as holiday gifts, rather than for small, incremental rewards, which other employee recognition programs notably offer.  Login integrations  with Google, LinkedIn, Facebook, Yammer, and other social platforms allow employees to quickly sign in to Reward Gateway's SmartHub without requiring them to manually create new accounts.  Segmentation  allows employers to easily distinguish between employees based on their roles, departments, locations, and other factors to effectively support performance and engagement.  UI and employee-specific customizations  let employers personalize experiences around teams' and individuals' unique needs. This personalized approach lets leaders prioritize specific goals, achievements, and behaviors while meeting each employee at their unique level.  Showcase vendors and rewards  you think employees are most interested in using Reward Gateway's SmartHub, and position this information somewhere enticing in the UI. This customization can further motivate employees by regularly reminding them of their recognition incentives.  Employee discount programs  let employers offer discounts and vouchers to big-name vendors and stores, which can drive greater motivation in employees who are more interested in monetary rewards. Brands include Expedia, Starbucks, Best Buy, Home Depot, Staples, GAP, Macy's, and more.  Support employees' mental, physical, and social health  by combining your employee recognition program with Reward Gateway's employee well-being programs. This program can help you foster a stronger, healthier culture by helping employees build emotional intelligence. However, it poses limitations compared to other higher-level wellness programs built for enterprise-scale businesses.   AI and Product Innovation Workhuman   Reward Gateway  The customizable interface  lets employers easily showcase the most important recognition data and the most enticing reward options, including cashback and discounts at popular stores.  AI-driven personalization  supports meaningful messages and change by guiding leaders through recognition processes, but the system isn't nearly as in-depth or innovative as other platforms.   Global Reach and Capabilities Workhuman  Reward Gateway   Global wellness options  allow you to offer well-being programs to remote and international teams. On-the-go and online features make health and wellness even more accessible, increasing participation and strengthening your company culture.  The unified engagement platform  consolidates recognition, communication, and more into its interface. This synchronization is especially crucial for hybrid, distributed, remote, and international teams, helping align communication and well-being regardless of employees' locations.  A unified points system  ensures that rewards uphold equal value in different countries, regardless of national currencies.  Support across 23 countries  enables international and remote teams to easily recognize employees while giving them ample choices for their rewards. However, this global reach isn't as expansive as in other larger employee recognition platforms, such as Workhuman.   Customer Support Workhuman  Reward Gateway     30-minute demos  let businesses see if Reward Gateway is a good fit before investing or fully implementing the platform, though the time window is very limited.  Client Support Teams  help HR leaders administer their platforms, customizing structures and reward systems around each business's unique needs.  A 24/7 help desk  offers both employers and employees live assistance and is accessible directly through brand-customized platforms. This way, users don't have to visit the Reward Gateway website or go out of their way to address issues.   Ease of Use & Implementation Workhuman  Reward Gateway  One-step logins  allow employees to quickly and securely sign in to their Reward Gateway accounts to read and share recognition, improving adoption and engagement. Users can also set up their accounts using their existing Google, Facebook, Yammer, or LinkedIn accounts for a simplified implementation.  "On the Spot" recognition tools  enable greater ease of use by letting leaders and employees quickly navigate the platform without adding more to their workloads. This design is particularly beneficial for frontline workers who rarely have time to sit down and scroll through web pages for several minutes at a time.  Reward expiration and technical issues  can make rewards challenging or impossible to use if employees don't fully understand them, stressing the need for effective implementation. For example, G2 reviews indicate that some users were not aware that certain rewards expire, resulting in the monetary value going unused and employees feeling unrewarded.   Workhuman vs. Reward Gateway: Strengths & Weaknesses Workhuman Strengths  Workhuman Weaknesses  Best suited for organizations seeking strategic, culture-building recognition, not for those seeking a simple gift card shop.  The partnership model includes consultation and coaching, which some buyers may view as more robust than necessary.  Reward Gateway Strengths  World-leading award redemption  provides employees with flexible redemption options and generally transparent pricing, though organizations may need clear communication around expiration policies to maximize value.  An   all-in-one engagement hub, consolidating recognition, rewards, communication, surveys, and more into a single platform.  Customization supports internal branding, recognition visibility, and motivation by showcasing the top rewards and other content employers want to prioritize.  On-the-spot recognition supports accessibility and ease of use for frontline workers.  Cashback, discounts, reloadable cards, vouchers, and other types of rewards further incentivize recognition processes.  Employees can create accounts and log in faster with one-step processes.  Reward Gateway Weaknesses  The pricing structure is better suited to large, enterprise organizations than to small or mid-market organizations, limiting cost-effectiveness and value.  AI integrations and other technical innovations aren't as advanced as those in other employee recognition platforms, limiting the insights you can draw from data.  Insights offer limited information into the reach of recognition or holistic employee performance, especially when improperly implemented.  Rewards and employee data may expire over time, limiting insights, motivation, and feelings of accomplishment.   Workhuman vs. Reward Gateway: What Customers Say    Customer Feedback & Quotes Workhuman:  Reward Gateway  "The pricing is really the only downside. I get that their platform is priced for large companies to use around the year, but we are just a small fry running a month-long step challenge." - Mid-Market G2 Enterprise Reviewer  "The platform made things very easy to facilitate and low maintenance for those that were overseeing the competition.... I felt like the team helping could have provided more insight on pros and cons for different features from past experiences instead of only positive reviews. Our company would have benefited from previous experiences as we ended up having to turn off certain features that became a hindrance during our competition." - Ashley A., Small-Business G2 Enterprise Reviewer  "Because our company is super competitive, it was not good for some people's mental health. I think there should be an option to take all stats off of everyone, and to only see your own. The admin can update everyone weekly instead of everyone seeing each other's numbers. Getting people up and outside walking. People who did not walk before are walking now because of this competition. It has a positive impact on most people in our company, with the exception of those who got too competitive." - Small-Business G2 Enterprise Reviewer  "Cost for access to the platform felt steep when you have to pay an additional cost to use said platform. Additionally, the way it was described for the Group Race feature it felt misleading. I had to completely customize every checkpoint along the way when I thought it was already done. I spent an entire day doing that. Meanwhile, we spent over a grand to utilize this platform. We did not get as much use out of it [as] we would like." - Small-Business G2 Enterprise Reviewer  "I would like to recommend [Reward Gateway] to remove the point expiration system. I have worked with several of [Reward Gateway's] competitors' plans, and none had a points expiration system. This benefited the employees using the system extensively because they never felt they could save up points for larger or smaller purchases during the Christmas season." - Byell J., Enterprise-level G2 Enterprise Reviewer  Price structures:  Many reviews express disappointment with the cost of Reward Gateway compared to its value, which is seemingly more suitable for large, enterprise-scale businesses than mid-market or small businesses.  Point expirations:  Certain Reward Gateway points and rewards, such as reloadable cards, expire after 60 days or 365 days, depending on multiple factors. Many reviews express disappointment with rewards that expire, which can make employees' accomplishments feel underappreciated and decrease future motivation.  Cultural fit:  Several reviewers noted that Reward Gateway was simply not a good cultural fit for them, whether due to their company size, their employees' motivators, or the types of insights it provided.  Why Workhuman Wins with Customers  Best-in-class analytics and AI:  Buyers and users regularly reference Workhuman’s analytics, reporting, and AI and Large Language Model (LLM) features as differentiators. These innovations help organizations demonstrate business value and drive engagement.  Genuine, human-centric recognition:  Users see Workhuman’s recognition as authentic and impactful, not just transactional.  Superior partnership and support:  Various customers highlight Workhuman’s flexibility, partnership approaches, and support throughout the buying and implementation processes.  Global reach and scalability:  Some of the world's largest enterprises trust Workhuman for its global capabilities and ability to scale recognition programs worldwide.   Workhuman vs. Reward Gateway: Final Verdict Choose Workhuman if:  Both Reward Gateway and Workhuman support accessibility and reward diversity in employee recognition. The best choice for you will depend on your company size, the types of rewards you're interested in, and the level of insights you want in recognition processes.   Choose Reward Gateway if:  You want to combine employee recognition with other programs and employee needs.   Reward Gateway consolidates employee communication, well-being, surveys, and discounts into its recognition platform, elevating insights and reducing the number of other tools you need to use.  You want a user interface that aligns with your brand image.   Reward Gateway's branded platform customizations let you add logos, company colors, and more to the platform's UI, elevating company culture and brand identity.  You want to offer monetary-focused rewards and recognition.   Reward Gateway's reward options include cashback, reloadable cards, and cashback to popular retailers, which may be more enticing to some employees.   Final Verdict  Both Workhuman and Reward Gateway can enable stronger employee recognition and leverage rewards to drive motivation. The difference shows up in insights, price, and culture.
