This broad scope can make it somewhat challenging to track and  improve employee experiences  over time. Human resources (HR) and leadership teams must adopt multiple tools and strategies, such as surveys, events, and episodic reviews, to holistically gauge employees' feelings. Digital employee experience (DEX) Digital employee experience is a more specific aspect of the employee experience, focusing on how  employees interact with digital technology.  DEX has received greater focus in the 2020s as more businesses shift to remote, hybrid, and distributed work models that use digital collaboration tools. Managing DEX is often easier than managing traditional experiences because the digital landscape supports continuous, embedded, and technology-enabled tracking. Tools and processes that contribute to the digital workplace experience include:  Where recognition and feedback fit into DEX Digital experiences have become a massive aspect of many modern workplaces. As a result, recognition, feedback, and celebration are now often digital-first experiences. Digital signals and insights, such as changes in productivity, can reveal how employees actually feel beyond what they say or do.  Tracking the right data with modernized tools will support your peer recognition, real-time feedback, and value reinforcement. Workhuman's ®  conceptual project,   Recognition Done Right™ ,  treats employee recognition as a  digital-first experience,  ensuring you don't overlook the DEX aspects of the employee experience. Consistent performance tracking enables continuous feedback rather than episodic performance reviews, providing reliable, real-time insights.  Benefits of investing in a better digital employee experience Digital employee experience (DEX) has become a primary driver of how work gets done. When most workflows run through apps, portals, and collaboration tools, small points of friction (slow load times, repeated logins, unclear navigation, inconsistent mobile access) compound into meaningful productivity loss and employee frustration. Tracking DEX helps leaders see where work stalls, where teams bypass approved tools, and where day-to-day experience is undermining engagement,  performance, and retention . Just as important, DEX is actionable. Unlike broad employee experience signals that can take months to interpret, digital signals can point to specific breakpoints you can fix: the workflow that’s causing rework, the tool that’s failing during peak usage, or the process that requires too many steps to complete routine tasks. Increased productivity A strong DEX reduces the “hidden tax” of context switching, workarounds, and interruptions. Clear, intuitive workflows help employees complete key tasks faster, with fewer errors, and with less reliance on training or manager support. The payoff is not just speed, but consistency: teams spend more time on value-creating work and less time troubleshooting basic processes.  Stronger engagement and connection In hybrid environments, connection is increasingly mediated through digital moments. Recognition, feedback, and shared rituals can  reinforce belonging  and purpose for remote workers, who aren’t in the same room. For example,  Social Recognition ®  from Workhuman ®  makes appreciation visible across teams, helping leaders reinforce impact, collaboration, and values in the flow of work.  Real-time feedback and performance reinforcement Modern digital work enables more frequent, in-the-moment coaching. Instead of waiting for scheduled review cycles, leaders can use timely feedback and recognition to reinforce effective behaviors and course-correct early.  When paired with  Human Intelligence™  (AI + recognition data), leaders can spot patterns that matter, like where collaboration is thriving, where recognition is uneven, or where teams may be at risk of disengagement. Lower operational and people costs DEX improvements can reduce ticket volume, cut time-to-productivity for new hires, and limit turnover driven by chronic friction. Strong digital experiences also reduce shadow IT by making the “right way to work” the easiest way to work, protecting security and compliance without slowing teams down. Better cross-functional collaboration When the digital workplace is coherent, collaboration scales. Employees can find information, align quickly, and contribute across boundaries without battling tool sprawl or inconsistent processes. Over time, that clarity supports faster execution,  better decision-making,  and more inclusive participation across locations and roles. Key elements of an effective digital employee experience A functional digital employee experience strategy must include several core elements, including easy accessibility, data security, and system-wide integrations. Alignment with business strategy DEX investments should complement your broader business goals, such as improving employee retention, performance, and company culture. For example, when investing in new hybrid work software, consider solutions that support both user experiences and your  organization's scalability . When providing employees with feedback, keep recognitions and goals aligned with your business's values and strategic priorities. Usability and accessibility  Integration and connectivity To streamline your digital workplace experiences, use platforms and solutions that integrate with your other daily tools. Digital workplace platforms such as Workhuman offer integrations with Slack, Teams, Outlook, and email to keep all communication in one,  easy-to-use interface.  This supports collaboration while avoiding disconnected experience layers. Recognition, feedback, and belonging are embedded in daily work Employee recognition isn't just "nice to have." Recognition, feedback, and belonging are core elements of the digital employee experience when they are embedded directly into daily tools employees already use. Recognition from leaders and peers can increase employees' visibility and equity, especially when supported by employee experience technology such as Workhuman Recognition Advisor™ and Social Recognition. Additionally, AI support can improve the quality of your recognition messages without adding friction. Data, insight, and culture intelligence Today's digital age requires leaders and HR to move beyond surveys and other traditional tools to track  engagement and culture . Now you can use real-time signals and data points from experience technology to continuously track and develop  strategies to improve employee engagement . Data from recognition tools and Workhuman's Inclusion Advisor can reveal gaps and strengths in your team's engagement. Use these insights to refine your company culture and engagement based on your team's unique needs. Security, trust, and privacy The  digital workplace tools  you use should be secure enough to protect all sensitive data your organization may handle. Employee, client, and customer data are protected by the Privacy Act and other laws, depending on your industry. Encryption and thorough cybersecurity will help you ethically manage data and maintain legal compliance. Additionally, disclosures of how data is collected and used support better  transparency at work .  Digital employee experience examples Digital workplace experiences vary based on your industry, organizational structure, employees, and business outcomes. Check out these examples of digital employee experiences in action. Example 1: Embedding recognition into daily collaboration A distributed workforce can leave you with various teams and workflows to track when providing feedback and recognition. It's easy to embed  employee experience technology  into collaboration tools for accurate, in-the-flow recognition. These personalized, actionable insights can increase participation, visibility, and engagement. Example 2: Using recognition data to identify engagement gaps Recognition data from digital workplace tools reveals gaps in engagement and performance. Leaders can track surface trends by team, region, and role to narrow down the exact issues contributing to low engagement. They can then enact targeted interventions to effectively improve retention, performance, and collaboration. Example 3: Scaling meaningful feedback with AI support Many  AI-supported tools  automatically analyze trends and patterns in employee engagement to provide a holistic understanding of their performance, backed by specific data. These insights can improve the quality of employee feedback at scale without risking manager overload.  How to design a strong digital employee experience strategy Follow these steps to develop a digital employee experience strategy based on your team's unique needs.  Step 1: Assess the current digital experience Consider the different technologies employees already work with, such as inventory tools, email accounts, and cloud storage. Identifying your experience touchpoints and workflows can offer crucial insights into the variables impacting your team.  Analyzing recognition participation and sentiment signals using Workhuman helps you understand how employees genuinely feel about their digital workflows and systems.  Step 2: Define clear objectives Once you understand the strengths and  gaps of your current digital workplace experience , set clear and measurable goals for your new experience strategy. Consider objectives related to employee productivity, engagement, belonging, retention, and culture change. Step 3: Engage HR, IT, and business leaders Redefining your organization's digital landscape shouldn't be a one-person job. Get business leaders, HR, IT departments, and other relevant departments involved in the experience design. This can establish shared ownership and help you develop an  employee experience strategy  that aligns with everyone's interests. Step 4: Select experience platforms, not just tools Searching for files across multiple apps, programs, and tabs can slow down operations, cause anxiety, and contribute to data silos. As you upgrade your technology, look beyond individual, single-purpose tools. Instead, prioritize integrated platforms that combine experience delivery with insight, such as with Workhuman's embedded recognition and feedback.  Step 5: Create a phased roadmap  Step 6: Provide enablement and support Everyone adapts to new company technology differently, so some employees may need a little more support than others. AI-assisted coaching reduces the burden of training and software onboarding while providing employees with the support they need. For example,  Workhuman's Recognition Advisor  supports in-the-moment coaching and guidance by providing actionable recognition and feedback.  Step 7: Monitor and continuously improve Relying on only annual snapshots or periodic reviews limits your ability to monitor improvement or identify the specific factors impacting employee experiences.  On the other hand, tracking real-time signals maximizes your insights into how employees are managing and feeling in their digital workplace environments. You can identify and respond to issues as quickly as they appear to maintain a productive, stress-free culture.   How to measure DEX As you establish objectives for your digital employee experience strategy, ensure that your goals are tangibly measurable. For example, instead of saying you want employees to "work harder," consider the objective metrics, signals, and key performance indicators (KPIs) you can use to track productivity. The following DEX metrics can be useful for  measuring job satisfaction  and refining employees' digital workflows. Technology performance signals KPIs related to  technology performance  gauge how your digital tools and solutions support or impair employees' experiences. For instance, an office's internet connection quality can significantly speed up or slow down its daily operations. Examples of technology performance signals include: Platform stability and reliability Device uptime and health Access history Network latency Crash and error reports IT ticket volumes Experience and behavior signals Recognition data provides continuous, behavioral insight into engagement, connection, and belonging. Additionally, tracking the frequency of and participation in peer-to-peer recognition offers crucial insights into peer visibility and cross-team recognition.  Other examples of experience and behavior signals include: Software usage and adoption data Performance and workflow trends Time spent completing tasks Participation rates Employee sentiment signals Unlike traditional surveys, recognition data reflects lived experience in real time. Pulse surveys, in-the-moment feedback, and other  employee sentiment strategies  provide more accurate, up-to-date DEX data.  Information such as the changing trends in pulse survey scores over time gives you insight into understanding and managing the human side of employees' experiences. Solutions like  Workhuman iQ™ / Human Intelligence™  can further help you turn employee sentiment signals into qualitative insights.  Business impact metrics Connect DEX trends to retention, engagement, onboarding time-to-productivity, and operational productivity measures (output per employee, cycle time, project velocity). Where possible, run correlation analysis between DEX scores and business KPIs. Finally, consider how AI-powered analytics can accelerate insight. Workhuman iQ and its AI Assistant surface cultural health signals, engagement patterns, retention risks, skills mapping, and on-demand reporting — along with personalized recommendations for managers and insights that link employee contributions to company values.  Calculating the ROI on your digital employee experience investment A credible DEX ROI model starts with a baseline (current ticket volume, tool usage, downtime, time-to-proficiency, and key workflow cycle times). From there, quantify costs and benefits conservatively and show payback over 12–36 months. Cost components Include software licenses, devices and infrastructure, implementation and integration services, training/change management, ongoing support, and internal project time. Hard benefit calculations Prioritize savings you can validate in finance terms:  Soft benefit calculations Model productivity gains carefully: minutes saved per day × employees × fully loaded hourly rate × workdays. TeamViewer found 80% of workers lose time to dysfunctional IT, averaging 1.3 days per month—use data like this to justify why small friction reductions add up. Example:  saving  5 minutes/day  for  2,000 employees  at  $50/hour  over  230 workdays  ≈  $1.9M/year  in capacity. ROI formula and reporting ROI % = (Total benefits − Total costs) ÷ Total costs × 100.  Also report payback period and (for multi-year programs) NPV with a risk-adjusted discount rate. Building a business case Lead with hard savings, then layer in productivity and experience outcomes. Use scenarios (conservative/base/aggressive) and tie improvements back to the business processes leaders care about: onboarding speed, cycle time, and retention risk. Understanding the DEX technology stack For leaders building a business case, it helps to view DEX as a stack, not a single purchase. The goal is a  great digital employee experience  that removes friction from everyday  business processes  and helps  empower employees  to do their best work—whether they’re in the office, remote, or hybrid. That’s why conversations around implementing a digital employee experience solution increasingly sit at the intersection of HR, IT, and security: the experience is shaped as much by integration and architecture as by any one tool.  And when the stack isn’t working, the cost is real—TeamViewer research, ‘  ’ found  80% of employees lose productive time  to dysfunctional IT, averaging 1.3 days per month. Infrastructure layer This foundation includes endpoint management (desktop computers, laptops, and mobile devices), connectivity (Wi-Fi/VPN), identity and security (SSO/MFA, endpoint protection), and digital workspace delivery (virtual desktops/browser-based workspaces). Reliability here is what makes a  seamless digital employee experience  possible. Application layer Next are the systems employees live in: communication (email/chat/video), collaboration, HR platforms (HRIS, learning, performance), and productivity suites. Tool sprawl and inconsistent access create detours in core  business processes —and that’s where adoption and engagement often break down. Experience and analytics layer This is where DEX becomes measurable and manageable: digital adoption guidance, experience monitoring, sentiment signals, and virtual support. Gartner, in ‘Digital Employee Experience Management Tools Reviews and Ratings’, defines  digital employee experience management tools  as solutions that improve employee sentiment and technology performance using near-real-time data from endpoints, applications, and context, including self-healing automation. Top DEX platform categories Common categories include UEM, dedicated DEX platforms, EXP suites with DEX modules, ITSM with employee-focused experience features, and standalone analytics. As per ‘The Great DEX-pansion Of 2025’, Forrester predicts continued market growth and consolidation as buyers push for more unified capabilities. How AI and automation enhance DEX AI helps  empower employees  through predictive issue detection, automated remediation (“self-healing”), and 24/7 virtual agents that resolve common requests quickly—supporting a  great digital employee experience  without adding headcount. DEX architecture: How components work together A practical architecture connects data collection (agents/APIs/telemetry) to aggregation (lake/warehouse), analytics (patterns, anomalies, prediction), and action (workflow triggers, fixes, self-service), then surfaces insights in role-based dashboards.  Integration is the difference between “more tools” and a  seamless digital employee experience :  Workhuman Cloud ®   offers packaged integrations with Workday (including Workday Cloud Certified Connect), Microsoft Teams, and Slack, plus open APIs and a lightweight design that reduces logins and workflow friction. Overcoming common digital employee experience challenges No system is perfect, especially when it comes to new technology. Fortunately, a proactive strategy can overcome common DEX hurdles.  Here are some of the most significant challenges of digital employee experiences – and how you can address them.  Fragmented technology stacks  Instead of continuously adding tools to expand your digital capabilities, consider integrating your experience layers to support unity, collaboration, and cohesiveness.  Low adoption and change fatigue With new technologies being introduced seemingly constantly across industries, employees may eventually grow tired of change. Design digital experiences around workflows and processes that employees actually want to use, and prioritize platforms such as Workhuman that stay up to date with the latest DEX technology. Additionally, use employee recognition as a natural driver when adopting new tools.  One-size-fits-all experiences While it might sound great to develop a single system that suits every employee's digital experience, this isn't always practical. Employees' needs vary by their role, location, strengths, preferences, at-home capabilities, and various other factors. While you may start your  DEX strategy  with a one-size-fits-all approach, you'll eventually need to tailor digital workplace employee experiences around each person's unique needs. Lack of actionable insight DEX metrics and KPIs aren't always directly measurable using traditional performance-tracking strategies. Instead, you will need to track various key DEX signals to record tangible data on employees' engagement, software adoption, and digital experiences. Move away from traditional surveys and towards continuous experience intelligence, such as with  AI-powered tracking  and analytics.   The future of the digital employee experience Even if you develop the perfect digital employee experience for now, it will still need to evolve to keep up with industry changes, artificial intelligence, and new technologies. Following the latest trends in digital workplace experiences will help you future-proof your DEX strategy.  AI-driven personalization AI-powered tools provide tailored recognition, feedback, and nudges based on each employee's unique responsibilities, goals, and needs. This level of AI-driven personalization can particularly support human resources by offering crucial tips for everyone on your team.  Strategies for implementing AI into HR include: Identifying  upskilling opportunities Prioritizing security and privacy alongside AI innovation Promoting the benefits of your DEX strategy to drive adoption Using dependable systems for employee management and recognition, such as Workhuman  Continuous culture intelligence According to ‘Organizational Culture - Cultural Change and Technology,’ a strong, adaptive company culture can support digital transformation and growth when adopting new practices. DEX tools are actively evolving to offer increasingly precise real-time visibility into engagement and belonging.  These insights can also support the continuous development of cultural intelligence to improve how your work culture interacts in  diverse cultural settings  and with individuals from different backgrounds.  Experience in the flow of work Your digital workplace experiences should enable employees to easily complete their daily tasks without interruptions or friction.  Modern DEX strategies are prioritizing fewer platforms and more embedded experience moments to streamline your access to information while preserving security and privacy. Prioritize platforms with intuitive,  user-friendly designs  that let you easily access all relevant tools and information for every project.  From programs to ecosystems Integration and synchronization are increasingly important for distributed, hybrid, and remote workforces. The right interconnected tools enable teams to easily share and access information, even when using different apps. This is especially crucial as technologies continue to evolve, as you may need to adopt more tools and workflows to keep up with industry trends.  FAQ How do you measure the success of a digital employee experience initiative? Use a balanced set of metrics: perception (DEX score, task effort), adoption (active use and proficiency), performance (uptime/latency/errors), digital friction (tickets, password resets, tool switching), and business impact (onboarding time, retention signals, productivity indicators). Segment by persona, location, and role so you can identify gaps that averages hide. How does digital employee experience impact remote and hybrid teams specifically? Remote and hybrid teams feel DEX more intensely because nearly every interaction is mediated through technology. When access is inconsistent, performance is unstable, or workflows require too many steps, it shows up as slower cycle times, more interruptions, and weaker connections. When DEX is strong, teams collaborate smoothly across locations, get help faster through self-service, and maintain shared rituals (like recognition) that reinforce belonging. Who is responsible for digital employee experience—HR or IT? Both. IT teams typically own infrastructure, security, and support operations; HR owns the  employee experience principles , listening strategy, and change enablement. The best model is a shared governance structure (often a digital workplace or DEX steering group) that aligns standards, prioritizes journeys, and resolves trade-offs between experience, cost, and risk. What is a reasonable timeline for seeing ROI from DEX investments? Expect a phased curve. Quick wins (like SSO improvements, workflow simplification, and self-service enhancements) can show measurable friction reduction within 30–90 days. Hard savings (ticket reduction, tool rationalization) often become clearer in 3–6 months, while retention and productivity benefits typically require 6–18+ months to validate. Baseline first, then report payback and run-rate value over time. What role do employees play in designing and improving DEX? A central one. Employees should help map high-friction journeys, validate priorities, and pilot improvements. Treat them as co-design partners (not just survey respondents) through focus groups, champions, and  feedback loops.  This increases adoption, reduces rework, and ensures you’re improving the workflows that matter most. How do you balance security requirements with a frictionless digital employee experience? Start with a principle: “secure by design, simple by default.” Use SSO and strong identity controls to reduce logins, apply conditional access so you only add friction when risk is higher, and measure the employee impact of security steps (authentication failures, reset frequency, time-to-access). The aim is security that protects data  without  slowing down the work you’re trying to enable. Wrapping up In the modern, technological age, investing in  digital employee experience  means investing in how your workplace actually feels. Done right, re-strategizing your DEX can streamline operations, support employee engagement, and improve collaboration and feedback between leaders, peers, and teams.  Workhuman's digital solutions offer crucial, real-time insights to help you understand employees' thoughts, refine experiences, and support adoption with continuous recognition.

title: 10 Effective Leadership Communication Skills Every Leader Should Master
teaser: Discover how leadership communication skills drive team alignment, trust, and better performance. Learn how to improve these essential abilities.
bodyText: Most leaders underestimate how much their communication style shapes team performance, retention, and trust. Research consistently links communication quality with leadership effectiveness ratings, yet many managers rely on instinct rather than intentional skill development. Leadership communication skills  are the verbal, written, and non-verbal methods leaders use to influence, align, and inspire their teams toward shared goals. These skills differ from general business communication through their emphasis on vision-casting, motivation, and stakeholder management rather than transactional coordination. This guide defines the four core pillars of leadership communication: clarity, active listening, empathy, and adaptability. You'll learn practical techniques for each pillar, discover how to assess your current strengths and gaps, and access actionable frameworks for developing these capabilities across your organization. Whether you're an HR leader designing development programs or a people manager working to strengthen your own effectiveness, you'll find research-backed strategies and real-world examples that translate directly into better outcomes for your team.  What is leadership communication?  Effectively communicating your mission , goals, and objectives motivates employees to fulfill their responsibilities with minimal oversight or management. Strong communication skills can also keep your team on the same page, reducing the risk of confusion, errors, or differing values. Key aspects of effective leadership communication Leadership communication skills are complex and multilayered, requiring you to consider various aspects of how you interact with employees. Explore the primary aspects of effective communication skills in leadership. Authenticity Leading authentically can  build trust  and improve your relationships with employees. Authenticity is about making sure your team sees you as genuine, honest, and consistent. You have to be aware of your personal strengths, weaknesses, and perceptions to ensure you're properly representing yourself. Focus on your relationship with employees by making time to socialize, get to know them, and share a little about yourself. Clarity An essential aspect of communication is delivering your message clearly and comprehensively. Clear communication will keep your teams aligned on goals, tasks, and values, and reduce the risk of mistakes or misconceptions holding back operations. Clear leadership communication focuses on the who, what, when, why, and how of every task you delegate. This means you must clearly define roles, establish objectives and deadlines, and explain the task's importance while being as specific as possible. Consistency As an effective leader, you must be able to "walk the walk" and back up your words with action. Consistency is about following through on your promises and goals, establishing that you're putting in as much effort as the rest of your team. It's also about  maintaining your standards and values , such as by not breaking rules or giving certain employees special treatment over others. For example, when adopting a new software or tool, take the time to learn how to use it effectively yourself before teaching your team. This gives you an opportunity to lead by example and prove that you're willing to do everything you're asking your team to do.  Transparency Transparency and honesty are crucial for building and maintaining trust with your team. Openly discuss the latest changes at your business, the reasoning behind decisions, and the challenges you're currently up against. This honesty can build mutual trust with employees and make them more likely to be open with you, including when addressing their personal challenges and concerns. Constructive feedback and dialogue Being able to effectively share constructive criticism and feedback is another  crucial communication skill  that can significantly impact your relationship with employees. Some people naturally handle rejection and negative feedback differently than others. Effective empathy and communication skills help you approach each conversation with sensitive, goal-oriented dialogue that makes each employee feel recognized and supported.  10 critical communication skills every leader must have Effective communication in leadership requires you to combine various skills and competencies. So what are the essential communication skills for today's market? Here are ten essential skills in leadership communication that you should know. 1. Active listening Effective communication  focuses on more than just sharing ideas. You must also listen to and digest others' ideas and perspectives, especially when leading a diverse team. According to research in the Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior, active listening skills can improve clarity, collaboration, and your relationship with employees.  These skills encourage you not just to hear what others are saying but to genuinely put effort into understanding their words and non-verbal cues without judgment. Take time to ask clarifying questions, and minimize distractions to show that you genuinely care about their perspective.  2. Emotional intelligence  3. Adaptability to different communication styles People communicate and listen in many different ways. For instance, some employees may require visual learning or verbal learning options when adopting new software and technology to effectively digest all the new information. Adapting to employees' unique communication styles is a key leadership communication skill. As an  inclusive leader,  you may need to adjust how you share information based on the audience and situation. Practice different types of communication in leadership, such as direct and authoritative or amiable and team-focused, to learn what works best for your team.  4. Feedback delivery Providing constructive, timely, and actionable feedback is a crucial leadership role. You can give feedback effectively by establishing trust, being specific, and framing criticism as  opportunities for improvement.  Focusing on employees' behavior rather than making criticism personal can make them feel safer and help them listen to what you actually have to say. Practicing healthy and constructive communication can also foster a culture of continuous feedback.   5. Body language According to the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley Library, the 55/38/7 formula suggests that only 7% of communication is delivered verbally. 55% is delivered through body language and 38% through paraverbal cues, such as your tone of voice. This stresses the need to be aware of your nonverbal communication and to recognize the potential meaning behind employees' facial expressions, tones, and body language.   6. Delegation skills At a basic level, delegation is about assigning responsibilities and tasks clearly based on each employee's unique strengths, goals, schedules, and other variables. Beyond that, effective delegation relies on clear communication to avoid confusion, motivate teams, and raise productivity.  As a leader, this often requires you to consider exactly how much you communicate with each employee. While you should comprehensively explain your reasoning and goals behind each task, you typically shouldn't micromanage every step of the process. Instead, trust employees and give them the autonomy to create their own personalized workflows.  7. Written communication Communication skills tend to differ between the spoken and written words. Written communication skills can help you  convey clear, concise, and effective messages  through emails, reports, and other written materials.  Written communication gives you more time to consider and revise every word you use to effectively get your message across. However, without nonverbal communication, readers may interpret your message in many different ways. For instance, sarcasm is difficult to identify when written, so employees may misinterpret sarcasm when you use it or wrongly believe you're being sarcastic when you're not. 8. Presentation and storytelling skills Being able to present information effectively and engage listeners is crucial for leadership, whether you're sharing details with employees, clients, or stakeholders. Practicing different ways to communicate ideas can help you adapt to different audiences, such as in meetings, conferences, and team briefings.  According to    , storytelling is a particularly powerful communication tool that lets you connect with others on an emotional and personal level. For instance, sharing how a new work process genuinely improves client or customer experiences can  motivate employees  to adopt it, because they'll understand why it's important.  9. Conflict resolution  10. Inclusivity Are you really having a conversation with your team if some members don't feel comfortable sharing their thoughts? Fostering a diverse and inclusive environment ensures that all voices are heard and valued in team discussions, establishing a sense of belonging and trust.  Tools such as  Workhuman's ®  Inclusion Advisor™  can empower employees to make communication more meaningful and inclusive by recognizing everyone's unique contributions.   Real-world examples: Good vs. bad leadership communication Even the “right” leadership communication skills can land the wrong way if the timing, channel, or phrasing is off. The examples below show how transparent, two-way communication builds trust during uncertainty — and how avoidance, inconsistency, or one-way messaging can quickly erode it.  Small shifts (private vs. public feedback, “here’s what we know” vs. silence, listening first vs. fixing fast) often make the difference between engagement and attrition. Example 1: Transparent communication during restructuring Setup:  A CEO anticipates a restructure that will include role reductions. Before individual notifications go out, she holds an all-hands to share the strategic rationale, the decision timeline, and what won’t change. She’s clear about what she can’t answer yet, and she names the emotional impact directly. What worked:  Employees heard the “why” early enough to avoid a rumor mill. The CEO balanced business reality with empathy: “Here’s what we know today, here’s what we’re still working through, and here’s how we’ll keep you updated.” She also opened two-way channels (office hours, anonymous Q&A, manager toolkits) so communication wasn’t just broadcast. Outcome:  Remaining employees report higher  trust in leadership  and less uncertainty-driven distraction — improving retention and engagement after the change. Example 2: Feedback that demotivated a high performer Setup:  In a team meeting, a manager calls out a top performer’s missed deadline as a “pattern,” without prior context or specifics. What failed:  Public criticism triggered defensiveness and shame, and the vague feedback (“be more proactive”) didn’t give the employee a clear path to improve. The manager also missed a crucial leadership move: separating the person from the problem and inviting dialogue. Better approach:  A private conversation, specific examples, and a co-created action plan (“Here’s what I observed; what got in the way; what support would help?”). Outcome:  The employee disengages and leaves within three months — a costly loss that started with a preventable communication misstep. Example 3: Active listening that prevented attrition Setup:  A director notices a usually engaged team member withdrawing. She schedules a 1:1 focused on listening, not performance. What worked:  She asks open questions, reflects back what she’s hearing, and validates feelings before problem-solving. Only after the employee feels heard do they collaborate on practical solutions (reprioritizing work, clarifying expectations, and agreeing on check-ins). Outcome:  The employee stays,  performance rebounds , and trust in leadership deepens. Why is effective communication important in leadership? Clear, healthy, and practiced communication plays a critical role in leadership effectiveness. As per ‘11 Ways Employee Recognition Builds  Better Managers’, as much as 70% of the variance in employee engagement can be attributed to their immediate supervisors, underscoring the direct impact of leadership communication on employees.   What are the benefits of good leadership communication?  From delivering feedback to delegating tasks, leadership communication skills support various aspects of management and human resources (HR) responsibilities. Explore the core benefits of these skills to understand why communication is so important in leadership. Sets the tone  Creates unity and purpose Effective communication can align teams by helping employees understand the significance of their work. For instance, an employee may be more likely to double-check their spreadsheets for errors if they recognize how much time the accounting team loses correcting mistakes.  Additionally, establishing a culture of open, honest communication supports collaboration and trust between employees, according to research in the Journal of Business and Management. A sense of unity can elevate productivity, morale, job satisfaction, and motivation, especially when working towards shared goals. Boosts morale and engagement  Transparent communication  builds trust, value, and purpose with employees while prioritizing clarity and specificity. An investigation in the Lakhomi Journal: Scientific Journal of Culture found that more transparent internal communication can develop a  stronger company culture  that supports employee engagement, morale, and motivation.  It can also give employees a stronger sense of belonging within your organization, making them more likely to engage with and support other colleagues and teams.   Clarifies expectations and reduces confusion Clear communication sets expectations early to avoid misunderstandings, misaligned goals, and other operational setbacks. Be sure to define specific roles, goals, deadlines, and anticipated outcomes. Create opportunities for employees to ask questions when sharing the information and throughout the work process. Additionally, share specific expectations in writing, over email, or with other tools to reduce the risk of employees forgetting or misremembering key details.  Builds trust and rapport Honest communication can strengthen your relationship with teams by building trust and unity. Beyond that, socializing with your team helps you  build organic rapport  and encourages them to socialize with each other, too. Practicing communication on easier days at work can then teach everyone how to communicate effectively with one another when solving problems or working under tight, stressful deadlines.  What are the hidden costs of miscommunication in leadership? Miscommunication can negatively impact your team and organization more than you might expect. These are a few ways that ineffective communication can impair your leadership capabilities.  Productivity anxiety and stress A lack of clear direction can leave employees confused about their responsibilities, their sense of purpose, and whether they're doing their jobs correctly. According to research by    , such misdirection and confusion can contribute to stress, reduced efficiency, and decreased employee well-being.   Distrust in leadership can also make it harder for employees to effectively digest feedback, take on new tasks, or believe the words you say. Stalled innovation and risk avoidance Poor communication can also hinder creative thinking. According to research in Revista de Gestão e Secretariado, employees will be more likely to  develop creative solutions  to problems if they understand all the goals and variables related to the issue. An open, judgment-free environment also helps make employees feel more comfortable brainstorming and sharing ideas. Furthermore, ineffective communication can encourage risk-averse behavior. For instance, an employee who negatively interpreted feedback about their performance may not feel comfortable trying a new approach to their work if they're worried about getting in trouble again.  Breakdown in team cohesion and collaboration  Frequent errors and rework Ineffectively communicating tasks, expectations, or processes can also contribute to mistakes and unnecessary rework. For instance, failing to explain how employees should format spreadsheets can result in sheets being written and interpreted differently. Communication-caused errors may negatively impact various aspects of your organization. For example, an incorrectly formatted order form could cause shipping delays, reduce inventory, and temporarily increase costs. A study in SSM - Qualitative Research in Health showed that  communication gaps  in healthcare can lead to diagnostic and treatment errors, potentially endangering patients' lives.  8 practical tips and best practices for communicating effectively as a leader Learning how to improve your leadership communication skills is a continuous process as you adapt to new employees, teams, and industry trends. Implement these actionable communication tips and practices to improve your  most important leadership competencies .  1. Set clear expectations Setting clear expectations with well-defined goals and guidance keeps team members aligned, even when working on different tasks. This can foster a shared understanding within your team and reduce the risk of errors. Key aspects of clear employee expectations include: Timeline:  Establish deadlines and the amount of time you expect them to reasonably spend on each task. Responsibilities:  Set fixed roles between team members to keep employees aligned and avoid duplicate work. Purpose:  Explain why the task is significant and how it supports your organization, team, and customers.  Quality:  Are mistakes, such as typos, acceptable, or should outcomes be perfect, finished product-level quality? Quantity:  Will they need to complete this task multiple times or create a specific number of outcomes? 2. Be clear and concise Clarity and brevity are crucial in leadership communication, but balancing both can be quite challenging. You want to be specific and comprehensive when sharing important information, but not at the risk of losing your team's attention.  Try combining written and spoken work to avoid unnecessary complexity while still delivering all essential information. For instance, when sharing progress at a meeting, you can use a presentation to showcase specific data. Alternatively, you could provide only a brief overview during the meeting and then send all the statistics and numbers later in an email for employees to browse on their own schedule. 3. Prepare ahead of time Preparing for leadership communication in advance can improve its effectiveness. Preparation strategies include: Taking time to understand your audience's needs and cultural backgrounds Tailoring your message around each unique individual Writing down and sharing your expectations and goals for the conversation Rehearsing dialogue in a mirror or with a colleague 4. Remove distractions for better focus Nonverbal communication is crucial for  effective communication . To promote this, try to eliminate distractions when talking to your team so they can focus on all cues. Strategies to reduce distractions and improve focus include: Encouraging active listening Limiting the use of phones during meetings Reducing background noise Introducing a "conversation ball" during group discussions Identifying tangents and practicing ways to steer the conversation back 5. Ask the right questions Asking the right questions enhances your leadership communication by letting you learn more about your employees and their workflows. Try asking open-ended or probing questions rather than short-answer or yes-or-no questions to encourage thoughtful, conversational responses. Asking questions can also show employees that you genuinely care about their perspective, further supporting trust and engagement. 6. Invest in ongoing leadership communication training  Effective leadership qualities  and skills must be regularly learned and relearned to maintain healthy dialogue and trust. Investing in  continuous leadership communication  training supports your long-term professional development and growth. More importantly, the right courses and programs can help you learn how to meet and communicate with your current team at their level. 7. Practice empathy According to research from Vaasa University of Applied Sciences, empathy skills help you identify employees' needs, recognize their nonverbal communication, and connect with them on an emotional level. This can build feelings of trust, safety, and comfort on your team, contributing to a more open and creative environment. Practice empathy as a leader by:  8. Reflect regularly on communication successes and failures Self-reflection is a powerful, ongoing practice for improving communication in leadership. It supports personal growth,  long-term leadership development , and your understanding of how others interpret your current communication style. Keeping a reflection journal, conducting regular self-assessments, and following other strategies can enhance your communication effectiveness over time.  Common leadership communication challenges and how to tackle them Explore the most common challenges in leadership communication and actionable strategies to overcome them. Balancing transparency with confidentiality Leaders should be transparent and honest when communicating with their teams without compromising confidential or sensitive information. Setting boundaries about what you can and can't share within your team establishes clear expectations and affirms that you're not hiding information dishonestly. Ensuring consistent messaging across different teams Delivering consistent messages can be challenging when working with different teams, departments, roles, and priorities. Establishing a centralized communication channel for key messages keeps teams aligned, even in remote, hybrid, and distributed environments. Navigating language barriers in diverse teams Language barriers naturally impair communication, especially in global or multicultural environments. Fortunately, you can easily mitigate potential comprehension errors by offering translation or language support. Additionally, encourage employees (and yourself) to minimize jargon and use visual aids when possible. Overcoming communication fatigue in teams According to an independent researcher    , communication fatigue caused by overloads of emails, notifications, and meetings can contribute to stress and limit the amount of information employees actually retain. Strategies to reduce communication fatigue include: Streamlining communication Prioritizing essential messages Limiting unnecessary meetings Encouraging team members to "unplug" when needed Breaking down information silos Information and data silos are the parts of your organization that isolate information and prevent it from being shared. Examples include personal laptops with important files not on the cloud or employees unwilling to share information with their teammates. You can break down these silos by unifying your communication channels, fostering cross-departmental collaboration, and encouraging transparency. Leadership communication skills for new managers The shift from individual contributor to people leader is one of the toughest career transitions — and many first-time managers are expected to figure it out as they go.  One widely cited data point: research referenced by Wharton, ‘Managing to Fail? Why New Leaders Need Training’, notes that  60% of new managers report receiving no training  when they step into their first leadership role, and separate research cited in the same piece says  60% fail within their first 24 months , often due to skill gaps that include communication.  New managers often lean on technical expertise to build credibility, but leadership credibility is also relational: setting expectations clearly, addressing issues early, and building trust through consistent, two-way dialogue. The good news is that you don’t need to become a “perfect communicator” overnight — you need a few repeatable habits that prevent avoidable missteps. Common communication challenges for new managers Balancing friendship with former peers while establishing authority:  Aim for warmth  and  clarity. Over-indexing on either creates confusion. Delivering constructive feedback for the first time:  Many managers avoid hard conversations altogether — a dynamic reflected in the research titled ‘Two-Thirds of Managers Are Uncomfortable Communicating with Employees’ is that  69% of managers are often uncomfortable communicating with employees , including giving direct feedback. Communicating decisions you didn’t make (or don’t fully agree with):  Don’t “spin.” Share context, explain what’s changing, and focus on what you  can  do for the team (support, resources, next steps). Managing up:  Practice translating team friction into business language: risks, trade-offs, and the specific ask you’re making. Quick wins for new manager communication  FAQ What are the most important communication skills for leaders? The most important leadership communication skills are the ones that consistently build trust and clarity.  In practice, that usually means: active listening, clear and concise messaging, emotional intelligence (empathy + self-awareness), giving and receiving feedback, setting expectations, and communicating through change.  Strong leaders also tailor their message to the audience and choose the right channel (1:1, team meeting, written update) so the message lands the way it’s intended. How can I communicate more clearly and concisely as a leader? Start by getting to the point early: lead with the decision, the “why,” and the next step. Use simple language, cut filler, and limit each message to 1–3 key takeaways. If you’re asking for action, be specific about  who  owns it and  when  it’s due.  A helpful quick check before you hit send or speak: “What do I want people to know, feel, and do after this?” How do I give constructive feedback without damaging relationships? Give feedback privately, promptly, and with specific examples. Focus on observable behavior and impact (not personality), and invite dialogue: “Here’s what I noticed, here’s how it affected the work, and I’d like to understand what happened.”  Then co-create a forward-looking plan: what “good” looks like, what support is needed, and when you’ll follow up. Done well, feedback strengthens relationships because it signals trust and investment. What role does Emotional Intelligence play in leadership communication? Emotional intelligence is what helps leaders communicate with both clarity  and  care. It shapes tone, timing, and how you respond under pressure.  Leaders with strong EI read the room, manage their reactions, and acknowledge emotions without getting derailed by them. That’s especially critical during change, conflict, or high-stakes decisions — when people need both transparency and empathy to stay engaged. Concluding thoughts: Why exceptional communication skills drive great leadership Communication plays various essential roles in great leadership, from establishing expectations to building a healthy rapport. Mastering communication is essential for leadership success, but it requires you to continuously learn and relearn various other soft skills, including empathy, emotional intelligence, and active listening. Workhuman can help you identify your team's strengths, skills gaps, and needs to further develop your leadership communication skills.

title: 28 Employee Appreciation Day Ideas for 2026 - Best Ways to Celebrate Your Staff
teaser: Looking for Employee Appreciation Day 2026 ideas? We’ve got 28 fun ways to mark the day and tips to make appreciation part of your company culture.
bodyText: Employers are always on the lookout for new strategies to motivate their employees. But the best way to spark that motivation is with a tried and true strategy already within their power: employee appreciation.  According to a Glassdoor survey titled '  ,' 81% of employees are more motivated to work harder when their boss shows appreciation. But it's not just linked to motivation. Engagement, productivity, and morale also get a boost with consistent employee appreciation. With  Employee Appreciation Day 2026  coming up, now is as good of a time as any for managers and business leaders to think about not only how to acknowledge and celebrate the day but also find ways to infuse appreciation more regularly. What is Employee Appreciation Day?  Employee Appreciation Day was created by Dr. Bob Nelson, a published author and founder of Recognition Professional International, as a way to strengthen the bonds between employers and employees and to remind leaders about the importance of showing employees they are valued. Why is celebrating Employee Appreciation Day important? Employees dictate the success of your company. It's not a stretch to say most employers would agree that the most effective way to achieve their goals is to have a workforce that is engaged, motivated, collaborative, and productive. All of those traits are boosted by employee appreciation. According to a  Workhuman-Gallup report , employees who report being recognized at their organization are 39% more likely to be engaged, 27% more likely to be thriving, and 45% more likely to agree they see a path to growth within the organization. Without employee appreciation, you'll be hard-pressed to find any gains in employee outcomes, and you'll be more likely to witness negative outcomes. Our research has found nearly 40% of employees are ready to look for a new job if they feel like they aren’t getting adequate and meaningful appreciation.   So, even though some may think telling employees “good job” from time to time is enough, the benefits that come from authentic appreciation – increased trust, motivation, and employee engagement – are undeniable. How to make National Employee Appreciation Day a meaningful moment The best way to make Employee Appreciation Day a meaningful moment is to not have it be the only time throughout the year that you are expressing appreciation to employees.  28 Employee Appreciation Day ideas to celebrate in 2026 Employee Appreciation Day is a chance to celebrate individual employees, teams, and the entire organization  and there are dozens of unique ways to celebrate Employee Appreciation Day at your organization. 1. Give employees a half-day Since Employee Appreciation Day always occurs on a Friday, consider starting a new tradition of giving employees the afternoon off so they can start their weekends early. For some, it gives them something to look forward to at the beginning of the week and motivates them to get their tasks done in the time available. 2. Promote peer-to-peer appreciation with recognition A formal employee recognition program gives colleagues the chance to join in on National Employee Appreciation Day and continue it throughout the year. By putting the power of appreciation into employees’ hands, we not only boost morale but also the trust between workers and their employers. Social recognition – which is most effective when there is a monetary value attached to it –  amplifies employee appreciation and relationships between coworkers  by creating a continuous loop of positive feedback in the workplace. 3. Plan a surprise Even though Dr. Nelson worked hard to get Employee Appreciation Day on the calendar, there are many workers who are likely unaware of the day altogether. And rather than use that lack of knowledge as an excuse to skip the holiday, use it to plan a surprise celebration. It could be music and balloons, a catered lunch with a dessert tower – you could even bring in trained therapy dogs to reduce employee stress. And for remote workers, a surprise gift card for lunch of their own helps keep everyone included. See also:  Workhuman vs Achievers Comparison Guide  4. Host a happy hour Happy hour doesn’t wait until five o’clock on Employee Appreciation Day. Log off an hour or two early and head out to a restaurant for some food and drink on the company’s dime. If your organization is small enough, you may be able to bring the happy hour to the office. Be sure wherever you are there are food options that align with any dietary restrictions and mocktails or alternative drinks available for fellow employees who don’t drink alcohol. This ensures there’s something for everyone without any discomfort or pressure. For team members working remotely, allow them to participate in a virtual happy hour. Send employees their favorite cocktail mix or a gift card.  5. Coordinate group activities Prior to Employee Appreciation Day, send out a list of suggested group activities for employees to choose from so their manager can plan in advance. Creative ways to involve the whole team include bowling, an escape room, or a scavenger hunt. Taking a field trip to enjoy local attractions such as a local museum, winery tour, or botanical garden is are great way to create a memorable day. Be conscious of choosing a group activity that involves team members interacting with one another and getting to know each other.  These activities aren’t just fun, they are also   beneficial for team building and collaboration . 6. Bring in a pop-up booth  When deciding on vendors, consider your company’s core values. For example, if your organization is active in DE&I efforts, consider supporting women-owned or minority-owned businesses. If the organization is based on sustainability, bring in eco-friendly brands. Many employees may even have side businesses of their own. Ask them if they’d be willing to share some of their own products. 7. Plan a Field Day Who says Field Day has to end after middle school? Divide employees up into teams and take the afternoon to play games and contests. Activities could range from a three-legged race and a water balloon toss to brain games, charades, and trivia. These  team games are a great opportunity for employees who don’t know each other to socialize and connect.  There’s nothing wrong with healthy competition, but try to keep it casual. The goal is to boost morale and fun. Unless your remote population travels to the office often, this suggestion may need some adjusting for virtual employees. Luckily, there are many team-building games that can be played right on your laptop, like virtual Guess Who? or Zoom Bingo. 8. Set up an office picnic Instead of work, how about a day in the fresh air with food and games? Activities that create random teams from across departments expand employee relationships. Take it one step further by inviting employees to bring a dish that holds significance to them, personally or culturally. A diversity potluck is an innovative way to show interest in your employees’ backgrounds and spark conversations among colleagues. Bonus: you get to eat great food. 9. Get your employees’ cars detailed If your workforce consists of mostly in-person workers, consider bringing in a mobile car detailing service to the office to spruce up their cars. Commuting to work isn’t fun, but doing it in a clean and fresh car makes it a little bit better. Send out a signup sheet for employees to fill out the week before the service is coming. That way, everyone gets a chance to take advantage, even if they aren’t in the office on the actual Employee Appreciation Day. You might also like:  25 Employee Appreciation Ideas That Actually Work  10. Record ‘thank you’ videos On National Employee Appreciation Day, take the time to create high-quality video messages to recognize employees for their hard work throughout the year.  One can be from the organization’s CEO, expressing their appreciation to employees for moving the business forward. Next, ask managers to produce their own personalized videos for direct reports. This moment of appreciation might include funny stories, specific personality qualities, or memorable moments that led to a positive outcome. And with an employee recognition program, employees can share these videos on a social feed for colleagues across the company to see and celebrate as well.  11. Create a team yearbook Create a digital yearbook to showcase employees’  celebrating a work anniversary , new hires, retirements, and more throughout the year. Jennifer Faulkner, VP of team member experience, diversity & inclusion, and talent management at Baystate Health says, “ Service Milestones  really reinforce emotional connection. These are personal revelations about the impact our people are having on one another’s lives.”  12. Promote wellbeing initiatives You can celebrate Employee Appreciation Day any which way, but if employees have low wellbeing it isn’t likely to make a difference. Employee wellbeing initiatives give your employees the chance to take a step back from work and focus on their mental wellbeing. Look to coordinate yoga or meditation breaks throughout the day for employees to take part in. For sustained wellbeing, consider continuing these practices on a bi-weekly or monthly basis so employees can continue taking time to focus on their wellbeing.  13. Have a volunteering day As per the    survey, 70% of working Americans strongly believe “volunteer activities are more likely to boost employee morale than company-sponsored happy hours.” And while happy hours are fun, volunteer opportunities give employees a deeper purpose and allow them to contribute in a meaningful way.  Whether it’s an individual or group of colleagues, volunteering somewhere local like a homeless shelter or humane society, creates a special moment of connection among peers.  Share photos and videos in a common place everyone in the company can see them. A social feed like the   Community Celebrations® timeline  extends the lifespan and impact of the event. Then, others in the organizations can see and comment on the noteworthy occasion their fellow colleagues participated in. 14. Host an Ask Me Anything meeting An  Ask Me Anything (AMA) meeting  is one where employees are able to submit questions to company leaders in an open forum. These types of meetings have become more common in recent years. Alongside the increase in discussions around psychological safety, they offer safe spaces to have transparent conversations without fear of judgment. This might not sound like much of a celebration, but it can be. In addition to work topics, questions can also aim to get to know company leaders on a more personal level. Questions can be silly, maybe a little embarrassing – as long as there is an employee moderator to keep things on track. 15. Send social media shoutouts In the week leading up to Employee Appreciation Day, use your organization’s social media channels to give shout-outs to employees who have gone above and beyond in their work. It’s important to acknowledge their impact for others to see, both externally and at the company.  16. Bring in a guest speaker Bringing in a guest speaker can provide a spark of inspiration and entertainment for the entire company. Take the time to talk with different members of your organization, especially those leading Employee Resource Groups (ERGs), to determine the subject of the talk and get recommendations for speakers. 17. Promote learning and development opportunities According to LinkedIn's 2022 Workplace Learning Report, 72% of surveyed professionals agree that Learning and Development (L&D) has become a more strategic function in their organization. With reimbursement options, employees can gain new skills from mentorship programs, certificate programs, and post-graduate degrees.  Many employees may not even be aware of these resources, which makes Employee Appreciation Day a perfect opportunity to share them. 18. Give out team awards Employee Appreciation Day is a day to celebrate individual and team accomplishments.   Team Awards  ensure your employees feel appreciated and highlight the importance of shared accomplishments across your organization, on the holiday itself and beyond. 19. Host a company-wide recognition event  Planning a company-wide recognition event is a powerful way to celebrate every team member’s contributions. Whether in person or virtually, these events create a shared moment of appreciation, boosting morale across the organization.  Take time to  highlight individual achievements, milestones, and the collective efforts that drive success . Not only does this make employees feel valued, but it also strengthens the sense of belonging and team spirit. When employees feel recognized on a larger scale, it fosters increased motivation, productivity, and a stronger connection to company goals. See also:  Workhuman vs AwardCo: Which is Better?  20. Provide department-specific celebrations  Allowing each department to plan its own Employee Appreciation Day activities gives teams the freedom to celebrate in ways that resonate with them. This approach fosters creativity and team spirit as employees tailor events to their unique culture and goals. It’s a great way to show that appreciation can be personalized, making everyone feel more connected and valued within their team. 21. Create an employee recognition wall  An employee recognition wall, whether physical or digital, is a great way to highlight and celebrate everyday achievements. Set up a board where employees can post notes of appreciation or shout-outs to their peers.    For a virtual version, consider using platforms like Slack or an internal social network to create a digital recognition board. To keep it engaging, encourage regular participation by designating a weekly “shout-out” time. The visual display of appreciation boosts morale, fosters a culture of recognition, and gives everyone a chance to be celebrated. 22. Organize a company-wide competition or challenge Engage employees with friendly company-wide competitions, such as a talent show, trivia contest, or fitness challenge. Offering fun, lighthearted events with prizes for winners can create excitement and camaraderie. Consider hosting a themed competition that reflects your company’s values or culture, allowing employees to showcase their talents or team spirit. This fosters a sense of fun and connection while motivating employees to participate and bond outside of their regular work tasks. 23. Personalized thank-you notes from leadership  Personalized thank-you notes from leadership are a simple yet meaningful way to show employees they are seen and appreciated. Taking the time to handwrite or craft thoughtful, individual messages can have a lasting impact on morale.   24. Turn it into Employee Appreciation Week Why limit appreciation to just one day? Extending Employee Appreciation Day into a full week allows for more diverse activities and ensures everyone’s contributions are recognized. You can organize themed days, team-building exercises, or workshops that cater to different interests and preferences.  A week-long celebration also allows employees to look forward to and actively participate in various events, making recognition feel more inclusive and comprehensive. It’s an excellent way to deepen engagement and celebrate employees in a variety of ways. 25. Give meaningful gifts Gifting employees something thoughtful and personalized can be a powerful way to show appreciation. Rather than generic gifts, select items that reflect your employees’ individual preferences or contributions – we dive into further detail in our gift-giving section below!  Meaningful gifts not only make employees feel valued but also reinforce the company’s appreciation, fostering stronger relationships and long-term loyalty. A well-chosen gift can serve as a tangible reminder of the company’s gratitude. 26. Host a virtual appreciation event  For remote employees, a virtual appreciation event is an excellent way to connect and celebrate their efforts. Host a virtual recognition ceremony where leaders can acknowledge achievements or organize online games and activities that promote engagement.  You can also host a virtual happy hour to encourage casual conversations and team bonding. The key is to ensure  remote employees feel included and connected to their colleagues , strengthening their sense of belonging and making them feel just as appreciated as those local to an office.  27.   Offer additional paid time off  Offering additional PTO is a thoughtful way to show appreciation. This extra time off acts as a reward for hard work and dedication while promoting work-life balance. A well-timed PTO offer can help employees recharge, boosting productivity and morale.  Whether it’s a “bonus” day off or a long weekend, giving employees the flexibility to take time for themselves demonstrates the company’s commitment to their well-being and helps cultivate appreciation for your organization, which breeds long-term loyalty. 28. Provide access to online wellness resources  Supporting employees’ well-being is an essential part of showing appreciation. Providing access to online wellness resources – like fitness classes, meditation apps, or mental health support – can help employees manage stress and maintain a healthy work-life balance.  These resources can promote overall wellness, reduce burnout, and improve job satisfaction. When employees know their employer cares about their holistic well-being, it strengthens their commitment to the company and fosters a positive, supportive culture. Thoughtful gift ideas for Employee Appreciation Day 2026 Donate on behalf of employees It’s always important to give back. Ask employees to donate to a cause they have an emotional connection with. This doesn’t necessarily have to be monetary – canned food, clothing items, raffle baskets - they can donate anything that sparks an uplifting moment for whoever is receiving the donation. Make sure employers are matching these donation efforts from employees. Reward employees this Employee Appreciation Day by supporting the causes they care about –  it’ll show them how much your organization cares about them. Send out gift certificates Every employee has different tastes and hobbies, which can make finding a one-size-fits-all gift difficult. Instead of spending time and energy trying to find a gift that takes culture, location, and personal preference into account, allow employees to choose their own gift. Compile a list of stores and restaurants local to your employee population and ask employees to choose one they would like to receive. Not only will they appreciate the gift certificate, but they will also appreciate the thought put into it.    Send a personalized care package Sending care packages to employees’ homes is a perfect opportunity to  say “thank you”  and a fun way to surprise employees. Create a bag of goodies with fun snacks, a backpack, or a water bottle – thoughtful  gifts for employee appreciation  paired with a personalized message to show your gratitude  This is a great option for organizations with dispersed employees or a largely remote workforce because they do not need to be in the office to be included. Personalized company merchandise  Adding custom touches, like an employee’s name or role, makes company merchandise feel personal and meaningful. Popular options include branded apparel, office supplies, or tech accessories.  Customizing gifts adds extra value, showing employees they’re recognized as individuals, not just part of the team. Experience-based gifts  Experience-based gifts, like local activities or dining experiences, offer employees the chance to create lasting memories. Unlike material items, experiences provide meaningful, long-term value and demonstrate thoughtfulness, leaving employees with memories that reinforce their connection to the company.  Wellness packages  Wellness packages, including fitness gear, relaxation aids, or healthy snacks, promote employees' physical and mental well-being. By encouraging self-care, wellness packages support a healthier, happier workforce and remind employees that their well-being is valued by the company. Tech gadgets and accessories  Tech gadgets and accessories make great gifts that show appreciation while supporting employees’ productivity and comfort. Consider items like wireless chargers, ergonomic tools, or noise-canceling headphones – tools that can enhance their work-from-home setup or office environment.  These gifts not only serve as practical, everyday solutions but also signal that you’re invested in helping employees perform their best. By providing the right tech, you create a more comfortable and efficient workspace, making your team feel supported and valued. Make employee recognition and appreciation a priority year-round As we’ve mentioned, saying ‘thank you’ and acknowledging your employees shouldn’t have to wait until Employee Appreciation Day – and it shouldn’t stop after it, either. Recognizing employees for their contributions and achievements makes them feel like they and their work matter to the company.  A Gallup survey found that employees who feel fulfilled from recognition are: 4x  as likely to be engaged Less than  one-half  as likely to be looking or passively watching for job opportunities 44%  more likely to be “thriving” in their overall life  Employee recognition is the way to make every day Employee Appreciation Day, as it demonstrates a consistent  language of appreciation  and their continued investment and commitment to employees. This inspires them to feel connected, confident and cared about. FAQs Why is employee appreciation important? Employees crave gratification for their hard work. Expressing appreciation for your employees is an authentic gesture that acknowledges their inherent value. Recognizing and appreciating employees has the power to resonate with them throughout their careers.  How do companies show employees appreciation? There are many different ways to show employees you’re appreciative of them and one of the best ways is to say thank you often and sincerely. This can be even more impactful with an employee recognition program, as it can be seen by other employees across the organization. What are the benefits of appreciating your employees? Appreciating your employees is a boon to their well-being and morale. It strengthens your company culture and makes the workplace more inclusive. It also just makes business sense. Gallup found that creating a culture of recognition can save a 10,000-employee company up to $16.1 million in employee turnover costs annually. Conclusion Employee Appreciation Day schedules time for gratitude on the calendar. It’s an honorary reminder to acknowledge what makes every business go: its people. You should show appreciation for your employees throughout the year – it's the only way that appreciation will be felt and genuinely meaningful. But you can kick Employee Appreciation Day celebrations up a notch. Planning to use an idea of ours? Snap a photo, then tag us on social ( @Workhuman ) so we can join the celebration!

title: Celebrating HR Professionals Day in 2026: Honoring the Backbone of Every Organization
teaser: Learn about HR Professionals Day and how to celebrate and appreciate your HR team’s role in boosting morale, engagement, and retention.
bodyText: When people know their work matters and that they are valued, they are more likely to be engaged, loyal, and perform better. A Gallup–Workhuman ®  study, ‘ Amplifying Wellbeing at Work and Beyond ’, found that  receiving   strategic recognition at work makes employees up to 90% less likely to report feeling burned out and up to 10× more likely to feel a sense of belonging.  So, how do you recognize your human resource team on  HR Professionals Day  in a meaningful way that shows their work matters? Your HR team shoulders countless daily responsibilities to keep your organization running smoothly. They work in the background to transform individual contributors into a cohesive, productive team. During the National HR Day, you can strategize your celebrations to strengthen connections and show HR team members they are a valued part of your company. What is HR Professionals Day? HR Professionals Day honors the hard work of human resources professionals and raises awareness of the vital role they play in every organization. It was established to appreciate professionals who:  On International Human Resource Professionals Day, you have the opportunity to pause and give a well-deserved shoutout to the hardworking HR team members. When is HR Professionals Day celebrated? September 26 marks HR Professionals Day worldwide. Not to be confused with International HR Day, which falls on May 20,  HR Professionals Day falls on Saturday, September 26 in 2026 . In fact, it is the same date every year, so you can mark your calendar for this annual HR professional appreciation day.  But the celebration is not only about appreciating employees on a single day. If you wait until September 25 to think about how to recognize your HR team, you’ve already missed the boat. Instead of treating it as a deadline, consider HR Professionals Day a checkpoint for recognition that’s already happening throughout the year. You may also like:  How to Celebrate Employee Appreciation Day  History and origins of HR Professionals Day Although the terms “welfare secretary,” “labor manager,” and “human resources” have been floating around for  more than a century , HR Professionals Day was first established in 2013. The idea was first introduced by a Jamaican Governor-General, Sir Patrick Allen. But it wasn't until 2018 that the day was  officially recognized  in Jamaica.
